Can this person safely do this job, and if not, what would make it safe?

Every visit in this clinic answers that question. These notes introduce a provider new to the clinic to the health system, the fundamentals of occupational medicine, the service lines, how the clinic runs, and Net Health, and stay useful as a reference after the first weeks. Working notes, not official clinic policy.

The University of Kansas Health System

The health system

Updated 2026-11-01

Two organizations, one name#

The University of Kansas Health System (TUKHS) is the clinical organization: the hospitals, the clinics, and the providers who work in them. The University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC) is the university. They share a name and sit side by side in Kansas City, KS, but they are separate organizations. The occupational health clinics are part of the health system.

The entities#

EntityWhat it isWhat it means in the clinic
TUKHSThe health system. Also called UKHA (University of Kansas Hospital Authority) or "the hospital." The hospital became an independent authority, separate from the university, in 1998. It joined with UKP in 2017 to form the health system.Its employees are an internal client: post-offer exams, Health and Wellness visits, and Employee Health. See TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams.
The University of Kansas HospitalThe main campus hospital in Kansas City, KS.The Medical Pavilion clinic is on this campus.
UKPThe University of Kansas Physicians, the physician group. Its physicians are employed by the health system, and many are KUMC faculty.A client with its own post-offer and results routing.
KUMCThe university: the schools of medicine, nursing, and health professions, plus research. It generally does not provide patient care.A separate client. Its results and letters route differently from TUKHS.
GMEGraduate medical education: residents and fellows. KUMC employs them (they're on the State Employee Health Plan); the health system funds many of the positions.A separate client in the routing tables.
Regional campusesHospitals and clinics that joined the system, such as Olathe Health (2023), Liberty Hospital (2024), St. Francis in Topeka (2017), and Great Bend (2018).Olathe and Liberty count as TUKHS for routing. Regional-campus employees sometimes come in for post-offer exams. St. Francis and Great Bend are handled locally, so we don't typically see their employees.

How results, clearance letters, and work status route for each client is in Where results and letters go.

Names you'll hear#

  • TUKHS, UKHA, "the health system," "the hospital": the same organization.
  • SW Market: the Olathe-area market. Its former Employee Health nurses are now part of TUKHS Employee Health. See Employee Health.
  • Medical Pavilion: the clinic on Olathe Boulevard in Kansas City, KS. It is not the Olathe clinic. See Our clinics.

The basics

Core Concepts

Updated 2026-11-01

Provider, employee, employer. The employer wants a safe, healthy workforce, care done right, and findings reported on time. The employee wants to be heard, kept safe, treated, and told what we found. Our role is to do both, and doing both is good for the employee, the employer, and the community. Every visit answers one question: can this person do this job safely, and if not, what accommodations would make it safe?

Your Role#

You are an objective observer who cares. Report what you see and measure, not what anyone hopes you will write. Caring and objectivity don't conflict; the observer who stays objective is the one everyone believes.

Be a gatekeeper, not a wall. See everyone who comes to you, and help them through safely. When the gate has to stay closed, tell them what would open it.

You are not their primary doctor. Examine and treat what the job or the injury calls for. If you notice something else, tell the worker and send them to their own doctor.

You are not judge or jury. Others decide whether a claim is covered, whether someone is hired, and what a case is worth; you give them accurate information so they can do their jobs. What you advocate for is the worker's safe return to work.

The Employee#

Assume the worker wants to work. Most want to be healthy, stay healthy, work, and provide for their families. Don't start from suspicion.

Treat the patient. A work injury gets a real diagnosis and real treatment. Start simple, and escalate without hesitation when it's needed.

First aid first. Most work injuries get better with over-the-counter medicine, ice, time, and a recheck. Prescription care is no better when first aid will do, and it makes the injury count on the employer's safety record. When the injury needs more, give it.

Keep them working. Time off is a treatment with side effects, and it is rarely the right one. The default is work with clear, specific restrictions, such as "no lifting over 20 lb," never "light duty."

Direct the care. You set the plan. Share it with everyone, and follow it until the worker is back to full duty. A work note from the emergency department or a specialist is information, not an order.

The Employer#

Know the job. You can't decide whether someone can do a job you don't understand. Read the job description, ask the employer, and ask the worker what they actually do.

Know the regulations, and follow them exactly. Where a rule sets the standard, as on a DOT exam, apply it as written; your opinion of the rule isn't part of the exam. Drug tests and surveillance exams follow fixed procedures, and a shortcut can void the result.

Match the person to the job. Compare what you find to what the job requires, not to a list of diagnoses. If a change would make the job safe, say so; whether the employer can make it is the employer's decision.

A diagnosis is not a reason to say no. Under the ADA, a person can be kept from a job for safety only when there is a significant risk of substantial harm to them or others that accommodation can't reduce. This is called a direct threat, and it has to rest on this person's current condition, not on assumptions.

Communication#

Communicate early and often. Tell the worker first, then call the employer at the first visit and whenever the plan changes. Report findings on time. The case that goes badly is usually the one someone heard about late.

Share only what each party needs. In an injury claim, the employer and insurer get the work-related diagnosis, work status, restrictions, and the plan. On a hiring or fitness exam, the employer gets function only, never a diagnosis. Anything unrelated to the work stays between you and the worker, on the phone as well as in writing.

Write the first visit for a stranger. Record what happened in the worker's own words: when, what they were doing, and what you found. Someone you will never meet will read it years from now, and those facts can't be rebuilt later.

Document to justify your recommendations. Every restriction, referral, and decision needs support in the note. A recommendation the note doesn't support won't hold up.

Practice choice: the treating boundary

This practice treats. It diagnoses, manages, sets work status, determines maximum medical improvement (MMI), and documents medical facts. It does not perform IMEs, assign impairment ratings, apportion causes, or write legal causation or prevailing-factor conclusions in a treating note. It collects drug tests but does not serve as the Medical Review Officer. Federal employees injured at work are covered by FECA, not Kansas workers' comp; they are recognized at intake and the claim is routed. A payer or attorney may offer to pay for an opinion this practice doesn't give. The fee doesn't change the answer.

Kinds of visit

Updated 2026-10-29

Name it in the first minute#

Each kind of visit changes what the provider owes, who gets the answer, and which mistake is waiting.

Treat: the injury visit

A worker was hurt at work. Diagnose, treat, set work status every visit, and drive toward recovery and return to work.

Lacerations, strains, eye foreign bodies, exposures.

The trap: the reflex day off, and a note that reaches for a conclusion about the claim.

Decide: the exam against a job

Can this person do the essential functions of this job, with or without accommodation? There is no published criterion; the job description is the standard.

Post-offer exams, return to work, fitness for duty.

The trap: examining a diagnosis instead of the job.

Certify: the exam against a standard

A regulation or named standard already set the bar. Examine against it and certify on the required form.

DOT drivers, respirator users, firefighters, police.

The trap: moving the bar, in either direction.

Watch: surveillance

A worker in an exposure program. What is the exposure doing over years? The baseline is the most important visit.

Lead, silica, asbestos, noise, bloodborne pathogens, TB.

The trap: turning it into a general health screen.

Visits blur. A post-offer exam for a truck driver is both decide and certify. An injury visit can turn up a surveillance finding. When that happens, each part follows its own rules.

The company protocol decides what you examine. It doesn't decide what you record: every finding you make goes in the note, asked for or not.

Any visit can end in a transfer#

The clinic doesn't monitor patients. A worker goes home with precautions or is transferred, never held in a room to see if they get worse. Decide on the category (the mechanism, the exposure, exertional chest pain), not a reassuring first look, and send the findings with the worker. The card, clearance, or specimen waits until the worker is safe.

Who's in the case

Updated 2026-10-28

Many readers#

Only the worker is in the room, but many people read the note.

The employee, employer, and provider share one goal: a healthy worker in a safe workplace. Everyone else works the claim around them. Medical determinations stay with the provider; authorization, compensability, and claim value stay with the others.

The parties#

PartyWhat they do
CarrierThe insurance company that bears the financial risk of the claim.
AdjusterManages the claim day to day. Authorizes care and needs timely work status.
TPAThird-party administrator. Runs claims for a carrier or a self-insured employer without bearing the risk; acts like an adjuster.
Self-insured employerPays its own claims instead of buying insurance, usually through a TPA.
Nurse case managerCoordinates care for the carrier, TPA, or employer. Helpful with scheduling; not a clinical authority over treatment, work status, or MMI.
HR, safety officerThe contacts for job descriptions and what modified duty actually exists.
Authorized treating providerIn Kansas the employer or carrier generally chooses who treats the injury. Often that's the clinic.
Attorneys, administrative law judgeAppear when a claim is disputed. A clean, factual record keeps the provider out of the fight.

What leaves the building

Updated 2026-11-02

Each party gets its piece#

Each party gets the piece of the case that belongs to it, and no one gets the whole chart. There are three lanes:

  • Workers' comp: no authorization needed, as far as the act allows. The claim gets what it needs, not the chart.
  • Findings the employer needs for its OSHA duties: may go if the worker had written notice at the time of care.
  • Everything else: only on the worker's written authorization, and its scope is the ceiling.

The worker always hears everything about their own care, and hears it first. The day something changes (an injury, a restriction, a referral, surgery, MMI), the employer knows, after the worker. Call the employer at the initial injury visit; a call that isn't documented didn't happen for anyone who wasn't on it. Most cases that go badly trace back to someone learning something after the fact.

What the employer gets depends on the service, and this is where new providers make the most errors.

ServiceThe employer getsThe employer doesn't get
Workers' comp claimThe work-related diagnosis, work status and restrictions with expected duration, the plan, and the medical causation judgment. The carrier or TPA gets the same, and the claim record on request. Kansas: reports on written request (K.S.A. 44-515(a)); records on request, with no release needed (K.A.R. 51-9-10).Anything outside the claim. Two injuries are two claims.
Post-offerWith written authorization: the clearance and functional restrictionsDiagnoses, findings, test values
RTW, FFDWith signed HIPAA authorization: capacity, status, restrictions or accommodations, and the functional basisDiagnoses (unless needed to explain a limitation, within the authorization), medications, treatment or psychiatric history, unrelated conditions
DOT examThe certificate (MCSA-5876): a non-CDL driver's to the carrier on request; a CDL or permit holder's only with consentThe exam report (MCSA-5875), unless the driver consents
Respirator clearanceThe written recommendation: able or not, limitations, follow-up, and that the worker got a copyThe questionnaire, diagnoses, spirometry values
Fire, law enforcementThe determination, functional impact, restricted essential tasks, and durationA diagnosis, except on written (not verbal) authorization. Fire behavioral health results never in identifiable form.
Hearing conservationWhether a standard threshold shift occurred and the OSHA recording criteria are metThe audiometric data in the clinic's record

HAZWOPERThe risk opinion and limitations; results only if the worker asksNon-occupational findings
Bloodborne exposureTwo statements: the worker was told the results, and was told of any condition needing follow-up. A hepatitis B vaccination opinion when the visit decided one.Diagnoses, lab results

All three: status, restriction, duration, and what return needs; a confirmed skin allergen with consent.Any opinion on whether ventilation, PPE, controls, or work-rest were adequate, or whether limits were exceeded. Never "overexposure."
PregnancyOnly if she wants the employer told: the limitation against the named agent or task, with durationThe pregnancy itself. Advice to leave an exposure goes to her, and she decides.

The most common disclosure error

The ADA's "functional terms only" limit applies to post-offer, RTW, and FFD exams. It does not apply to a workers' comp claim. Withholding under it there is the error.

  • Personal susceptibility, not injury: no claim. The employer gets the restriction, not the condition.
  • An ambiguous request: ask for the authority behind it. Don't guess, and don't refuse by reflex.

Where this clinic sends results, clearance letters, and work status for each client is in Where results and letters go.

Who pays

Updated 2026-11-01

The kind of visit decides#

Nobody hands over an insurance card. The kind of visit decides who pays, and intake settles it before the provider walks in.

KindVisitsWho pays
DecidecertifywatchPost-offer, RTW, FFD, DOT, respirator, surveillanceThe employer, as the clinic's client. No insurance claim.
Not an examDrug and alcohol testingThe employer, as the clinic's client. No insurance claim.
TreatInjury visitThe claim administrator: a carrier, a TPA, or a self-insured employer. Billed to the workers' comp claim and confirmed when the employer approves the visit.
TreatInjury to a federal employeeFECA, through the worker's agency. Routed out of the Kansas system at intake.

Things that come up#

  • On an accepted claim, the injured worker never gets a bill. No copay, no deductible, no balance. That's the clinic's practice. Kansas law itself is narrower: the worker can't be billed above the fees the director approves. A payment dispute is between the clinic and the claim administrator.
  • Settle payment at intake, not at billing. Confirm the claim administrator and billing recipient when the visit is approved.
  • Authorization refused. If the employer sends a worker and then won't authorize the visit, the evaluation still happens. Intake records who declined, when, how, why, and the claim contact; "employer said no" supports nothing. Kansas: an employer that sends an employee to find out whether a complaint is work-related pays for that visit (Kansas Schedule of Medical Fees, introduction).
  • The worker's own-choice allowance (Kansas: up to $800, K.S.A. 44-510h(b)(2)) is the worker's election, not a fund to send them into.
  • Wrong body part or side. The provider's evaluation defines the injury. Don't hold the visit for a referral that named the wrong part or side; document what you find. The correction goes to the employer and carrier before the first bill does. See Work comp visits.
  • A disputed bill (Kansas): the payer gives the specific reason within 30 days of the bill; the clinic has 30 days to request reconsideration, then an informal hearing before the director. Undisputed amounts are paid within 60 days. Once an application for hearing is filed, the bill can't be sued on or sent to collections until the claim is decided (K.S.A. 44-510j). The intervals move; check the statute when it comes up.
  • The Kansas fee schedule sets the maximum fee; a lower agreed fee supersedes it. Furnishing care under the act binds the clinic to those fees.
  • Occupational disease is the hard routing call. An acute injury plainly bills to comp. A condition built up over years of exposure may not, and whether it goes to comp or group health is decided by others from the facts the provider documents.

Diagnosis codes

Updated 2026-11-02

Exams come first, findings second#

An administrative exam is coded with a Z00, Z01, or Z02 code, listed first (ICD-10-CM Guidelines I.C.21.c.15). A finding at the exam is added as a second code (I.C.21.c.12). These codes aren't used when the visit is to diagnose or treat; code the problem instead.

Use the most specific code the visit has. Z02.89 is only for an administrative exam with no code of its own. An audiogram, a vision screen, a TB test, an immunization, or an exposure coded Z02.89 is miscoded.

KU's picks, including the ones the code set leaves open, are in ICD-10 codes.

Codes by visit#

VisitCode
Post-offer examZ02.1
Fire: post-offer examZ02.1
Fire: annual examZ02.89
Police: post-offer examZ02.1
DOT examZ02.4 (some groups use Z02.89; see Quick reference)

Hearing exam or surveillance audiogramZ01.10; Z01.118 with findings
Vision examZ01.00; Z01.01 with findings
Drug or alcohol test, post-offer: at the exam or on its ownZ02.1
Drug or alcohol test: reasonable suspicion, random, return-to-duty, follow-upZ02.89 for urine or breath; Z02.83 for blood
Drug or alcohol test after an accidentThe injury first if one is treated, or Z04.2 if injury is ruled out; then Z02.89 (Z02.83 for blood)
Worker who seems impaired, evaluated clinicallyThe findings. The visit is diagnostic, not administrative (I.C.21.c.5).
Antibody titer (hepatitis B, MMR, varicella)Z01.84, not Z01.89

Chest x-ray to show freedom from active TB, prior positive on recordZ11.1

Positive IGRA, no active TBR76.12

ImmunizationZ23
Behind on required vaccinesZ28.39, with Z23 when a dose is given
Rabies pre-exposure vaccinationZ23
Rabies exposureZ20.3. Add Z29.14 when HRIG is given and Z23 for the vaccine. A bite wound is coded first.
Pertussis exposureZ20.818 (meningococcal: Z20.811)
Blood or body fluid exposureZ77.21
Workplace asbestos exposureZ57.2, with Z77.090 to name asbestos

A worker with symptoms is coded to the symptom; the visit is diagnostic, not screening (I.C.21.c.5).

Z29.14 is the immune globulin only; the vaccine is Z23. Z01.89 (other specified special examination) is for a routine exam of one body system with no code of its own; an exam an employer or a standard requires is Z02, and a titer is Z01.84. Occupational exposure is coded to Z57; Z77.090 can be added to name the agent (Excludes2).

Z11.7 or Z11.1

The Index points two ways. Screening, tuberculosis, latent leads to Z11.7, but Test, tuberculin and Test, Mantoux lead to Z11.1. Z11.7 holds because an Index code must be checked in the Tabular List (I.B.1), and Z11.1 there is screening for active TB. A payer reading the tuberculin entry may still expect Z11.1.

What the code set doesn't settle#

  • Urine or breath test. Z02.83 names blood, and no code names a urine or breath test, so an administrative urine or breath test is coded Z02.89. A post-offer test is Z02.1 because the code names the reason. A collection invoiced to the employer, with no claim, rarely puts this in front of a payer.
  • A positive result. At a collection the clinic doesn't code a result: the MRO verifies it and reports it to the employer, and a presumptive positive on an instant cup isn't a finding until it is confirmed. A result the clinic reads itself is coded R78.- for blood (Z02.83 says to add it) and R82.5 for urine.
  • Periodic exam of a current employee. Z02.1 is pre-employment only, and the Index has no periodic, surveillance, or occupational exam entry. The nearby codes are Z00.00 (general adult exam), Z02.89, and Z13.88 (screening for a disorder due to exposure to contaminants). Z13.88's Excludes1 note sends a worker exposed with no suspected disorder to Z57.-.

A payer's or contract's coding instruction overrides a clinic's pick.

ICD-10-CM reissues every October 1 and can update in April. These codes were read from the FY 2027 release.

Employment laws

Updated 2026-10-28

Recognize which one is in play#

A new provider doesn't need to master these laws, only to recognize which one a question is about.

ADA: what an employer may ask, and when#

The Americans with Disabilities Act sets three stages. Where the worker is decides what medical questions are allowed.

  1. Before an offerNo medical questions or exams. The employer may only ask whether the applicant can do the job's functions.
  2. After a conditional offerA medical exam is allowed if everyone entering that job category gets it and results stay confidential. Withdrawing the offer needs a job-related reason consistent with business necessity, or direct threat. This is the post-offer exam.
  3. Once employedExams and questions must be job-related and consistent with business necessity. This is RTW and fitness for duty.

The ADA covers employers with 15 or more employees. The Kansas Act Against Discrimination (KAAD) runs parallel to it but covers employers with 4 or more, private or public. Apply ADA-level discipline to every employer.

Two ADA terms come up often:

  • Essential functions: the job's fundamental duties, the ones the exam is measured against. The employer names them and decides whether an accommodation is reasonable; you assess the person against them.
  • Direct threat: a significant risk of substantial harm that a reasonable accommodation can't remove. It is the only safety basis for saying no, and it has to rest on an individualized assessment of this person, not a diagnosis.

Medical information the employer receives is kept confidential and separate from the personnel file.

GINA: no family history#

The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act bars employers from requesting genetic information, and family medical history counts. The family history section of a family practice intake form does not belong in a post-offer exam. When an employer requests medical information, it should include GINA's "safe harbor" notice telling the provider not to collect genetic information. If the provider learns it anyway, it isn't part of what the employer receives.

PWFA: pregnancy limitations#

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (2023) covers employers with 15 or more employees. It requires reasonable accommodation for known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth, or related conditions. It comes up in pre-placement, restrictions, and return to work. The provider describes the functional limitation; the accommodation decision is the employer's. Separately, Title VII bars excluding a woman to protect a pregnancy; accepting a reproductive hazard is her choice (see The pregnant worker).

FMLA: the clock you don't see#

The Family and Medical Leave Act gives up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave. It isn't a disability benefit. Employers often run it alongside a comp claim, so work-status notes become the FMLA record without anyone saying so. An employer who gets insistent about a slow recovery around weeks 10 to 12 is watching the job-protection clock; that isn't a medical question. An employer can't make the clinic's evaluation the condition for returning someone from FMLA leave; that certification belongs to the employee's own provider, and no second opinion is allowed. When the 12 weeks run out mid-claim, job protection ends while comp continues. FMLA forms don't come to this clinic. A worker on FMLA leave may lawfully turn down light duty.

HIPAA: the workers' comp exception#

HIPAA allows disclosures needed to comply with workers' compensation law, so the employer, the carrier, and the TPA can receive claim-related records without a signed authorization. The permission covers what the claim needs, not the whole chart, and doesn't extend to anything else. For non-comp exams, what goes to the employer is defined by the program (the certificate, the written opinion) or by the worker's signed authorization. See What leaves the building.

Route-aways: spot them at intake#

  • Federal civilian workers, including postal workers, are covered by FECA, not Kansas workers' comp. A nurse practitioner or physician assistant is not a FECA "physician."
  • Railroad workers are covered by FELA, a negligence action, not workers' comp.
  • Longshore, harbor, and shipyard workers are under the federal Longshore act. The worker chooses the physician, and the treating physician's first report goes to the employer and DOL on its form within 10 days of first treatment.
  • Seamen are under the Jones Act: no workers' comp, but a negligence suit plus maintenance and cure, owed regardless of fault until maximum cure.

For all of these, no state apparatus (authorization, fee schedule, deadlines, forms) applies. Your medicine and documentation don't change. See Cases we don't handle.

Which state's rules apply depends on the rule. OSHA follows the worksite, workers' comp follows the claim, licensure follows where the patient is (telemedicine included), and DOT follows interstate commerce. Ask which state's claim it is.

One worker, three lenses

A lost-time back injury puts one person under workers' comp (compensation), FMLA (job protection), and the ADA (accommodation) at the same time. Three decision-makers, three clocks, one set of medical facts. An accurate note serves all three without being written for any of them.

Exposure limits

Updated 2026-10-08

The terms#

These acronyms appear on Safety Data Sheets, OSHA standards, and industrial hygiene reports.

TermSet byBinding?Meaning

RELNIOSHNoRecommended exposure limit. Often lower than the PEL.
TLVACGIHNoThreshold limit value. Professional guidance, widely used, frequently updated.

STELHow limits are expressedShort-term exposure limit, usually a 15-minute average.
CeilingHow limits are expressedA level never to be exceeded, even briefly.
IDLHNIOSHNoImmediately dangerous to life or health. Escape-or-die concentrations.
SDSManufacturerRequiredSafety Data Sheet. Sixteen standard sections; section 11 is toxicology, section 4 first aid. Ask for it on every chemical exposure.

The industrial hygienist#

An industrial hygienist measures the workplace: air sampling, noise dosimetry, ventilation. The provider evaluates the person. When a case depends on how much exposure there actually was, the industrial hygienist's data is what settles it.

Recordable, reportable, compensable

Updated 2026-10-29

Three different questions#

Three questions, decided by different parties, under different rules. An injury can be any combination of the three. The provider decides none of them, with two exceptions on the OSHA log: whether a case is a new case or a recurrence, once the employer asks (29 CFR 1904.6), and whether a hearing loss is work-related (29 CFR 1904.10; see Hearing tests).

The provider documents the medicine once; each party decides its own question from it. Recordable but not compensable, or the reverse, is no contradiction. Every covered employer must report, even one exempt from keeping the log. An admission counts; observation or testing alone doesn't. You may tell the employer a clock may be running.

Compensability runs on two Kansas tracks: accident and repetitive trauma (K.S.A. 44-508), and occupational disease (K.S.A. 44-5a01). Repetitive trauma never goes on the disease track. Knowing them helps route the bill to comp or group health; it isn't license to pick one in a note.

Kansas public employers are outside OSHA. With no state plan, federal OSHA, recording and reporting included, doesn't reach Kansas cities, counties, school districts, state agencies, or their fire, EMS, police, and public-works departments (29 U.S.C. 652(5)). Their comp claims are still compensable. A written opinion or letter to them never cites an OSHA standard as a binding legal requirement. A public hazmat team is the exception (see HAZWOPER). Whether KUMC and the health system count as public employers is an open question; see Kansas.

The first-aid line runs through the provider's pen#

An injury is recordable if it causes death, days away, restricted work or job transfer, loss of consciousness, a significant diagnosed condition (a fracture, for example), or medical treatment beyond first aid. OSHA's first-aid list is exclusive: anything not on it is medical treatment.

First aid (not recordable by itself)Medical treatment (recordable)
OTC medication at OTC strengthAny prescription, even one dose; OTC drugs at prescription strength
Bandages, butterflies, Steri-StripsSutures, staples, tissue adhesive
Hot or cold therapy; non-rigid supports such as elastic wrapsRigid splints or devices to immobilize
Tetanus immunizationPhysical therapy, chiropractic care
Eye foreign body removed by irrigation or cotton swab; eye patchForeign body removed with a needle, spud, or burr
Splinter removal by simple means; draining a blister; drilling a nailSplinter or foreign body removal by more than simple means
Massage; fluids for heat stressAnything else not on OSHA's first-aid list

X-rays and other diagnostic tests are neither. They don't affect recordability.

Restrictions are their own trigger. A restriction the provider recommends on a routine job function, or on the full workday, past the day of injury makes the case recordable even if the employer ignores it. A recommended day off counts as days away even if the worker comes in. A restriction for the day of injury only doesn't count.

Treatment is chosen clinically, and the log follows, never the reverse. Most work injuries belong on the first-aid side: OTC anti-inflammatory, ice, time, and a recheck. That's the better medicine, not a favor to the employer; avoid the reflex prescription that buys nothing. When the injury needs a prescription or sutures, give them. Under-treating to protect the log is the worse error. Employers will ask "can we keep this first aid?" The treatment you'd choose anyway is the answer.

The state report#

In Kansas, the employer reports to the state within 28 days of knowing of an injury that disables the worker beyond the day or shift (K.S.A. 44-557). The clinic doesn't file it. Sending work status and findings out the day of the visit is what lets the employer file on time. The treating physician reports to the employer or carrier periodically, at once on request, and on the day of release to work, and a copy of any return-to-work report goes to the worker at once (K.A.R. 51-9-10).

Kansas

Updated 2026-11-01

OSHA and public employers#

  • Kansas has no OSHA state plan. Federal OSHA covers private employers only. Cities, counties, school districts, state agencies, and their departments (fire, EMS, police, public works) are outside OSHA's standards and its log.
  • No Kansas rule stands in for the bloodborne pathogen, respirator, or hearing standards, so a written opinion for a public client doesn't cite them as binding. Public employees' injuries are still covered by the comp act.
  • KUMC and the health system are very likely public employers too, so outside OSHA. KUMC is part of a state university. The health system is a hospital authority created by statute (K.S.A. 76-3304), a public agency under the Kansas Open Records Act, and listed by CMS as government-owned (hospital district or authority). The health system adopts OSHA's standards by policy.
  • HAZWOPER is the exception: an EPA rule extends it to public hazmat teams, volunteers included (see HAZWOPER).
  • Kansas has no heat, ergonomics, or exposure-limit standard of its own.

Workers' comp#

The act's rules are in General and triage. The employer, not the treating physician, files the accident report, and the injured worker owes nothing above the director's approved fees (see Who pays). Kansas has no comp drug formulary.

Reporting to KDHE#

ClockWhatRoute
4 hours, phoneSuspected human rabies, active TB, measles, mumps, rubella, meningococcal disease, or novel influenza A. Any cluster, outbreak, or unusual illness.Epidemiology Hotline 877-427-7317, 24/7 (option 5 for TB, outbreaks, and rabies consults). For TB and the vaccine-preventable diseases, fax the form after the call.
24 hoursNew HIV, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C. Latent TB on a positive skin test or IGRA, before the chest x-ray. Pertussis or varicella on suspicion. Every quantifiable blood lead result, whatever the value. Carbon monoxide poisoning.Kansas Reportable Disease Form with labs, fax 877-427-7318, or to the county health department (Johnson County: online at https://diseasereporting.jocogov.org or fax 913-826-1300). HIV through KORDS or fax 785-559-4228. Blood lead at keap.kdhe.ks.gov.
  • The duty is yours, even if a lab or infection control has also reported, and whatever state the worker lives in.
  • A 24-hour deadline on a weekend or holiday moves to 5 p.m. the next business day.
  • An exposure to HIV or hepatitis isn't reportable; a new infection is. A single case of skin disease, heat illness, or pneumoconiosis isn't reported. Cancer goes to the Kansas Cancer Registry within six months.
  • Report every vaccine to KSWebIZ unless the person objects.

The full list: KDHE Disease Reporting for Health Professionals.

The local picture#

TB incidence is below the national rate; the 2024 Kansas City, Kansas outbreak is over and isn't the baseline. Alpha-gal syndrome occurs here. Ticks and tularemia: Zoonoses and tick-borne infection.

Employment, drug testing, prescribing, records#

  • The KAAD covers employers with 4 or more employees, so apply ADA-level exam discipline to small employers too (see Employment laws).
  • No Kansas statute sets which employees an employer tests or when; written policy does. Testing for Schedule I or II drugs needs a KDHE-approved lab; whether that reaches an occ med clinic's on-site screen is unsettled. Marijuana is Schedule I, with no medical carve-out.
  • Checking K-TRACS is voluntary, except that Kansas Medicaid requires a check before prescribing controlled substances to its members. Board of Pharmacy guidance bars searching anyone who isn't your patient, prospective employees included.
  • Keep patient records at least 10 years from the date of service.
  • Referral to an entity you hold a 10% or larger stake in requires written disclosure.

Reference

Glossary

Updated 2026-10-29

Terms#

TermMeaning
Accommodation (reasonable)A change to the job or workplace that lets a qualified person do the essential functions. Whether one is feasible is the employer's decision.
ACGIH, BEIAmerican Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists, a private nonprofit, and its biological exposure index: a level in blood or urine. Advice, not law.
ACIPAdvisory Committee on Immunization Practices. Its recommendations govern every vaccine indication, schedule, and contraindication, though which are legally in effect is contested in 2026.
ACOEMAmerican College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine. Its guidance (lead removal levels, law enforcement guidance, treatment advice) is recommendation, not law.
Action levelExposure level, below the PEL, at or above which (usually for a stated number of days a year) an OSHA standard requires monitoring and surveillance. Asbestos has none.
ADA (Title I)Americans with Disabilities Act. Title I covers employers of 15 or more: no medical exam or disability question before a conditional offer, and limits on exams of current employees.
AdjudicatorThe official who decides a disputed comp claim on the whole record, legal causation included. The note supplies the facts.
AdjusterManages a claim day to day for a carrier or TPA; authorizes care.
AggravationA lasting worsening of a prior condition. Recorded apart from a new structural change or a temporary flare that returns to baseline.
AHJAuthority having jurisdiction, such as a fire department or police agency.
Alternative vision standardFMCSA's route for a driver who fails vision in the worse eye (49 CFR 391.44): an eye specialist's MCSA-5871 and a card of 12 months at most. It replaced the vision exemption.
ApportionmentDividing the cause of a condition between work and non-work factors. Not done here.
Authorized treating providerKansas: the clinician the employer or carrier designates to treat the injury. Once a worker is sent here, the clinic is the ATP for the course of treatment, and its work-status opinion is presumed determinative.
B ReaderPhysician certified by NIOSH to classify chest x-rays for dust-related lung disease using the ILO system. Required for silica; one of three permitted readers for asbestos.
BATBreath alcohol technician, trained to perform DOT breath alcohol tests.
BeLPTBeryllium lymphocyte proliferation test. A confirmed positive means sensitization, not disease.
CCFCustody and Control Form that follows a drug test specimen from collection to lab.
CDL, CLPCommercial driver's license, commercial learner's permit. For holders, proof of DOT medical certification is the electronic state record, not the paper card.
CIRSChronic inflammatory response syndrome. Like "toxic mold syndrome," not recorded as a diagnosis.
Claim administratorWhoever runs a comp claim and pays the bill: a carrier, a TPA, or a self-insured employer.
ClearinghouseFMCSA's database of commercial drivers' drug and alcohol violations.
CollectorTrained person who collects a urine specimen following Part 40 procedures.
Conditional offerA job offer contingent on the medical exam. No exam, health form, or disability question before it.
Contract of serviceKansas: the employment relationship that makes someone a worker under the comp act. Decides whether an applicant hurt during a post-offer test is covered.
Declination (hepatitis B)The OSHA form a worker signs to decline hepatitis B vaccination. The worker can change their mind later at no cost.
DERDesignated employer representative: the employer's contact for drug and alcohol testing. Decides whether a refusal occurred.
Determination PendingDOT outcome that holds the decision up to 45 days for more information. Not available for a missing MCSA-5870 or MCSA-5871.
Direct threatADA term: significant risk of substantial harm that accommodation can't reduce. Requires an individualized assessment.
EEOICPAEnergy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act: federal compensation, run by DOL, for Department of Energy and atomic-weapons-site workers with cancer.
Essential functionsThe fundamental duties of the job; what the exam is measured against.
FCEFunctional capacity evaluation. Structured testing of physical capacity, usually by a therapist, that the provider orders and reads. Data, not a verdict; its recommended work level isn't the work status.
FECAFederal Employees' Compensation Act; workers' comp for federal civilian employees, postal workers included, run by DOL's OWCP. An NP or PA is not a FECA "physician."
FELAFederal Employers' Liability Act: the negligence system for injured railroad workers. Not workers' comp.
FFDFitness for duty: evaluation of a current employee whose employer has a documented, objective concern about safe performance.
First aid (OSHA)The exclusive list of care that does not make an injury recordable.
FMCSAFederal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, part of DOT. Sets the commercial driver medical standard and runs the National Registry.
FMLAFamily and Medical Leave Act: 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave. The return certification comes from the employee's own provider.
GINAGenetic Information Nondiscrimination Act. No family medical history in an employment exam, from the provider or the intake form.
HAZWOPERHazardous waste operations and emergency response (29 CFR 1910.120; construction, 1926.65). Surveillance for cleanup, treatment-facility, and hazmat-team workers.
HBIG, HRIG, VariZIGHepatitis B immune globulin, human rabies immune globulin, varicella-zoster immune globulin.
HBsAb, HBsAgHepatitis B surface antibody (10 mIU/mL or more after a documented series means immune); surface antigen (positive means infection: stop the series).
Hearing conservation programWhat OSHA requires in general industry at 85 dBA as an 8-hour average (29 CFR 1910.95): a baseline audiogram within 6 months, annual tests, and follow-up of an STS.
IGRA, TSTTB blood test (interferon-gamma release assay; preferred, and BCG doesn't affect it); tuberculin skin test (millimeters of induration at 48 to 72 hours; two-step at baseline).
ILO classificationThe International Labour Organization's system for classifying chest x-rays for dust disease. Used in asbestos and silica surveillance.
IMEIndependent medical examination: a one-time evaluation hired by a party to reach conclusions about a claim. Not done here.
Impairment ratingA percentage of whole-body function lost, used to value a claim. Not done here.
Industrial hygieneMeasuring and controlling workplace exposures. Whether a building or an exposure is safe is its question, not a clinical one.
Injury track, occupational-disease trackKansas: accident and repetitive trauma (K.S.A. 44-508) versus occupational disease (K.S.A. 44-5a01). Repetitive trauma never goes on the disease track.
Intoxication defenseKansas: an employer's defense to a comp claim based on a drug or alcohol test. Valid only if the test is admissible and an employer-collected specimen meets all six statutory conditions (K.S.A. 44-501(b)(3)).
K-TRACSKansas's prescription drug monitoring program.
KAADKansas Act Against Discrimination. Parallels the ADA but covers employers with 4 or more employees, private or public.
KCCKansas Corporation Commission. Regulates intrastate commercial drivers and grants their waivers.
KDHEKansas Department of Health and Environment. Reportable conditions go here.
KDOLKansas Department of Labor. Offers small private employers free, confidential OSHA on-site consultation.
KORDSKansas Online Reporting Disease System: KDHE's online route for reporting HIV.
KP&FKansas Police and Firemen's Retirement System. Its presumption is a pension rule, not workers' comp; the provider gives no opinion on it.
KSCPOSTKansas Commission on Peace Officers' Standards and Training. Certifies officers on a purely functional medical criterion (K.S.A. 74-5605(b)(7)).
KSDEKansas State Department of Education. School bus drivers meet the DOT clinical standard on its own forms, before hire and at least every two years.
KSWebIZKansas Immunization Registry. Every vaccine dose is reported to it unless the person objects.
LTBILatent TB infection: infection with active disease ruled out. Carries no work restriction by itself.
MECMedical Examiner's Certificate: the DOT card a qualified driver carries.
Medical causation, legal causationWhether the work event or exposure caused the condition, which is the provider's to call; applying the state's compensability test, which is the adjudicator's.
Medical removal protectionOSHA provision (lead, for example) that removes a worker from a specific exposure on a test result while protecting pay and seniority. A regulatory removal, not a disability; earnings are protected only where the standard says so.
MMIMaximum medical improvement: the condition is stable and not expected to improve with more treatment.
MROMedical Review Officer: a physician who reviews lab drug results and interviews the donor before the result goes to the employer. Not done here.
NFPA 1580The National Fire Protection Association's fire service medical standard (2025). Binds a department only if adopted. Restrictions name its essential job tasks, 1 to 15.
NIOSHNational Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, the federal occupational health research agency, in CDC. Makes recommendations (RELs, the lifting equation, heat guidance) and certifies B Readers.
Non-responderHepatitis B: anti-HBs under 10 mIU/mL after two complete series, not one. No third series.
NRCNuclear Regulatory Commission. Sets radiation dose limits for its licensees; Kansas, an Agreement State, applies its own.
NRCMENational Registry of Certified Medical Examiners; only examiners listed there can perform DOT exams.
Nurse case managerCoordinates care for a carrier, TPA, or employer; not a clinical authority.
ODGOfficial Disability Guidelines. Kansas: the fee schedule's measure of presumed medical necessity. Care beyond it isn't barred, but the note makes the case.
OPIMOther potentially infectious materials, under the bloodborne pathogens standard.
OWCPDOL's Office of Workers' Compensation Programs. Runs FECA (no carrier or TPA) and the Longshore act.
PAPRPowered air-purifying respirator. If a negative-pressure respirator would put the worker at risk and they can use a PAPR, the employer must provide one.
Part 4049 CFR Part 40: the federal procedures for DOT drug and alcohol testing.
PEL, REL, TLVOSHA's permissible exposure limit, the legal limit, many of them outdated; NIOSH's recommended exposure limit; ACGIH's threshold limit value. The last two are advice, often lower.
PEPPost-exposure prophylaxis: treatment after an exposure (HIV, hepatitis B, rabies, measles, and others) to prevent infection.
PLHCPPhysician or other licensed health care professional allowed by license to perform an OSHA-required evaluation, such as respirator clearance.
Prevailing factorKansas legal test (K.S.A. 44-508(g)): whether work was the primary factor, compared with all others, in causing the injury. Decided by the adjudicator from the facts the provider documents; a treating note never states a conclusion on it.
PUMP ActPUMP for Nursing Mothers Act: the federal workplace lactation law that governs in Kansas.
PWFAPregnant Workers Fairness Act (employers of 15 or more). Requires accommodation of pregnancy-related limitations, with minimal documentation.
RADSReactive airways dysfunction syndrome: lasting asthma after a single high-level irritant exposure, with no sensitization.
REAC/TSRadiation Emergency Assistance Center/Training Site at Oak Ridge. Radiation emergency consultation 24 hours a day; after hours 865-576-1005.
RecordableAn injury the employer must enter on its OSHA 300 log.
ReportableA severe outcome the employer must phone in to OSHA directly.
Risk, capacity, toleranceThe basis for a restriction: the probability of harm, measured ability, and the worker's willingness to work through symptoms. Tolerance alone isn't a basis.
RTWReturn to work: the employer wants independent confirmation, against the actual job, of a treating clinician's clearance before full duty.
Safety-sensitiveA job where sudden incapacitation or impaired alertness would endanger others: non-DOT drivers, forklift and crane operators, armed security, unprotected heights.
SCBASelf-contained breathing apparatus.
Scheduled injuryKansas: an injury compensated by a set schedule for the body part (vision or hearing loss, for example), not as whole-body disability.
SDSSafety data sheet: the manufacturer's hazard document for a chemical. Ask for it on every chemical exposure.
State planAn OSHA-approved state program that replaces federal OSHA and may cover public employers. Kansas has none.
STSStandard threshold shift: an average hearing change of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear compared with baseline.
SurveillancePeriodic exams that track the effect of a specific exposure over time.
TPAThird-party administrator that manages claims for a carrier or a self-insured employer.
TTD, TPD, PPDTemporary total, temporary partial, and permanent partial disability: workers' comp wage-benefit categories. Set by the adjuster, not the provider.
Two-step TST, boosted reactionA baseline skin test repeated after a negative first step; a positive second step, which reflects old infection, not a new conversion. Never two-step after an exposure.
VOMSVestibular/Ocular Motor Screening. Record the values and the change from baseline, never "VOMS positive."
WFIIAFF/IAFC Wellness-Fitness Initiative. Source of a treadmill fitness protocol for firefighters: a fitness test, not a stress test.
Work conditioningTherapy focused on strength, endurance, and flexibility for return to work.
Work hardeningInterdisciplinary program that simulates the job and addresses physical, behavioral, and vocational barriers.
Written authorizationThe worker's signed authorization to release information outside the comp and OSHA lanes. Its scope is the ceiling.
Written opinionThe limited report an OSHA standard requires the clinician to give the employer after a required exam.
ZPPZinc protoporphyrin: a marker of lead's effect over the prior weeks to months, drawn with a blood lead level.

Diagnostic Screening

Vision screening

Updated 2026-10-28

What it is#

Can this person safely do this job with their current vision, with or without correction? The visit ends in a clearance determination, with a referral when one is needed. It isn't eye care.

Confirm the standard first#

Don't default to 20/40 because that's the DOT number. Each exam has its own standard.

ExamStandard
DOT20/40 in each eye and with both eyes, a 70° horizontal field in each eye, and recognition of red, green, and amber signals
FireNFPA 1580, where the department has adopted it
Law enforcementThe certifying body's or agency's standard, or ACOEM's law enforcement guidance if there's none. Stricter than DOT; passing one doesn't satisfy the other. Kansas peace-officer certification sets no numeric vision standard, so the thresholds are the agency's.
Everyone elseOSHA has no general vision standard. The employer's written requirement governs; get it in writing before the exam. With none, test what the job uses and decide on direct threat.

What trips people up#

  • Test and record each eye separately. A good result with both eyes open can hide a failing eye.
  • Failing the color plates doesn't fail a DOT driver. Do a practical signal-color test and document both results.
  • A DOT driver who fails in the worse eye may be certified under the alternative vision standard. An eye specialist completes Form MCSA-5871, your exam must begin within 45 days of its signing, and the card is capped at 12 months. The vision exemption program no longer exists. See DOT certification.
  • Lenses: if correction is needed to meet the standard, note it. For DOT, put "wear corrective lenses" on the certificate. Bioptic telescopes aren't allowed for commercial driving.
  • A referral is not a determination. If the standard is met, refer and clear. If it isn't, refer and defer.
  • Depth perception alone doesn't fail a DOT driver or a post-offer applicant unless the employer has a written requirement. A poor result is usually procedure or an explained finding, so re-test first. A new or unexplained loss is referred.
  • Abnormal contrast sensitivity with normal acuity can be early eye disease. Refer to ophthalmology even when the standard is met.
  • The employer gets the clearance and any restriction ("corrective lenses required"), not test values or diagnoses.

Kansas drivers#

Intrastate commercial drivers (K.A.R. 82-4-3g) and school-bus drivers (K.A.R. 91-38-6) are held to versions of the federal rule that predate the alternative vision standard. For a driver who fails in the worse eye, check with the KCC or KSDE whether they'll accept it; don't assume. The KCC also has its own intrastate waiver.

Hearing tests

Updated 2026-10-29

One test, three questions#

QuestionWhat the audiogram answers
Hearing conservationHas a noise-exposed worker's hearing changed from their own baseline?
DOTCan the driver hear well enough to drive?
Workers' comp hearing-loss claimDocument the exposure history and the audiogram pattern. Cause goes to the retained expert, not to you. This is an exception to the rule that medical causation is the provider's (see Injury to MMI).

Hearing conservation (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95)#

  • The trigger is noise at or above 85 dBA as an 8-hour average. The testing rule covers general industry only. Kansas: public employers aren't covered. Test them the same way under contract, but don't cite 1910.95 as binding.
  • Schedule: a baseline within 6 months of first exposure (before exposure is better), then annual tests. A retest within 30 days can confirm a shift.
  • Standard threshold shift (STS): an average worsening of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear compared with baseline. The employer notifies the worker in writing within 21 days. Unless a physician finds the shift isn't work-related, the employer also fits, trains, and requires hearing protection.
  • The OSHA log takes an STS only if all three are true: an STS, a total hearing level of 25 dB or more in the same ear, and work-relatedness. You determine the components; the employer records.
  • The physician, never a technician or software, reviews problem audiograms, confirms an STS and whether it's recordable, decides work-relatedness and referral, and decides any baseline revision. A revision is never automatic.

Before you read the audiogram

  • The worker needs 14 hours without workplace noise before the test, or hearing protectors worn in its place, which OSHA allows. Record which. If neither, reschedule.
  • Look in the ears first. Wax or infection can mimic a shift.
  • Asymmetry is a referral question before it's a noise question. Criteria vary: the NHCA refers at 40 dB or more between ears at any frequency; AAO-HNS uses a pure-tone average difference over 15 dB.

Two choices OSHA leaves open#

OSHA lets hearing protectors stand in for the quiet period, and permits age correction. NIOSH advises against both. Age correction can push a real noise-induced shift below 10 dB, so look at the unadjusted shift too, and never age-correct the 25 dB component.

Practice choice: reading the audiogram

No age correction.

DOT#

The driver hears a forced whisper at 5 feet or more in the better ear, or has a better-ear average loss of no more than 40 dB at 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz. Hearing aids are allowed.

Convert modern audiometer readings first: subtract 14, 10, and 8.5 dB at those three frequencies, then average. Skipping it fails drivers who meet the standard. A driver who fails both methods isn't certified; tell them about FMCSA's hearing exemption.

Kansas workers' comp#

Hearing loss is a scheduled injury with no presumption of causation. On the repetitive-trauma track, a physician telling the worker the loss is work-related can set the date of injury.

Respirator clearance

Updated 2026-10-28

What it is#

The medical evaluation an employer must provide for every worker required to wear a respirator, before fit testing and before first use (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134). It starts with the confidential OSHA questionnaire (Appendix C). For most workers the questionnaire is the whole evaluation. Add an exam or spirometry when an answer, the work, or the respirator calls for one; a "yes" to the medical-condition questions in Part A, Section 2 requires a follow-up exam.

It isn't fit testing. Clearance asks whether the worker can safely wear a respirator. Fit testing checks whether a specific model seals.

Kansas has no state plan, so the standard binds private employers. State and local government employers aren't covered. Evaluate their workers the same way, but don't call it legally required in writing.

A firefighter's NFPA 1580 clearance is a separate determination (see Fire and law enforcement). How the form is handled in Net Health is in Respirator exams.

When you'll see it#

  • A new hire who needs a respirator, or a current employee never evaluated
  • Re-evaluation: symptoms related to respirator use; a request from you, a supervisor, or the program administrator; program information showing a need; or a change in conditions that may substantially add physical burden
  • Voluntary use of any respirator other than a filtering facepiece (dust mask)
  • Not just because the employer switched clinics

Health care workers on N95s, industrial workers on air-purifying or supplied-air respirators, and SCBA users all come through. It's often done with an asbestos or silica exam.

Spirometry#

  • Read it against the lower limit of normal (LLN), not the fixed 0.70 ratio or 80% of predicted, unless a governing standard sets its own metric (cotton dust, NFPA 1580).
  • Name the reference set on every report.
  • Never clear on invalid or non-repeatable spirometry. Read the curves yourself.
  • A 15% drop in FEV1 from the worker's own baseline warrants investigation, even within normal limits.
  • Late-term pregnancy is a relative contraindication to spirometry. Pregnancy alone isn't a re-evaluation trigger.

The written recommendation#

The employer gets only the determination (cleared, cleared with limitations, not cleared, or deferred for workup) and the limitations. Never the questionnaire, a diagnosis, or a spirometry value. The recommendation states:

  • Any limitations, made actionable: name the respirator type ("PAPR only"), and state exertion limits with OSHA's work-effort levels (light under 200 kcal/hour, moderate 200 to 350, heavy above 350), not "avoid heavy exertion"
  • Whether follow-up is needed, and the re-evaluation interval you recommend (OSHA sets none)
  • That the employee was given a copy. This is the element most often missed.

If a negative-pressure respirator would put the worker at increased risk and you find they can use a PAPR (powered air-purifying respirator), the employer must provide one.

Don't clear blind

Don't clear against work demands you don't know. Don't accept an employer's "voluntary use" label without confirming the respirator type.

Employer Health

Pre-placement exams

Updated 2026-10-28

What it is#

An exam after a conditional job offer. It decides whether an applicant, or an employee moving into different physical demands, can safely do that job's essential functions, with or without accommodation. It is job-specific, not a general health screen.

It is

  • An exam against one job's essential functions and demands
  • The component tests that job calls for
  • A history and exam aimed at what the job requires

It isn't

  • A family practice or internal medicine physical
  • Health maintenance or screening for unrelated disease
  • Family history

How the visit runs in Net Health is in Employment exams. TUKHS and UKP specifics are in TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams. The legal background is in Employment laws.

No offer, no exam

Examining before a conditional offer is an ADA violation, whatever the intent. Even handing over the health history form counts. Offer status is confirmed at registration. If it isn't confirmed, stop and send the applicant back to registration.

Three tiers#

The job category's confirmed demands set the tier. Tier 1 is the base; add 2 and 3 where the demands meet them.

TierJobsWhat it adds
1. BaseSedentary or light work, nothing safety-sensitive: office, call center, light retailConditions that limit the job's tasks; gait and mobility; a targeted exam where the history points. Vision or hearing only where the work uses them.
2. Physical demandMedium to very heavy work: warehouse, construction labor, custodial, patient handlingPast injury in the regions the job loads, exertional symptoms, hernia; BP, pulse, heart and lungs; strength and range of motion; functional testing only up to the confirmed demand
3. Safety-sensitiveJobs where sudden incapacitation or impaired alertness would endanger others: non-DOT drivers, forklift and crane operators, armed security, unprotected heightsFull medication list, OTC and cannabis included; seizure, fainting, sleep disorder, hypoglycemia, arrhythmia, vertigo; BP, pulse, heart and lungs; a neuro screen; vision for driving or equipment

Regulated components (DOT, respirator, hearing, NFPA, HAZWOPER) are added by the job at any tier, each under its own rules. An employer's uniform protocol may add more, but a finding outside the job's demands can't support a screen-out.

Outcomes#

  • Cleared
  • Cleared, noting a non-essential limitation
  • Cleared with an accommodation recommendation
  • Not cleared, naming the affected function or an individualized direct-threat assessment

No exclusion by diagnosis or age. Fear of future injury or comp costs isn't a basis. The employer makes the hiring decision.

The employer gets the determination and functional restrictions, within the applicant's written authorization. No diagnoses, findings, or values, except on regulated forms.

Rules that keep the exam clean#

  • Don't clear against a job you don't understand. Request the job demands and hold the determination. Confirm a demand that looks wrong (a 120-pound lift), and test only to the confirmed demand.
  • Everyone entering the job category gets the same exam. Extra follow-up for one applicant only when it's medically related to that exam's findings, never for age, appearance, or body size. Flag referrals that look hand-picked.
  • No family history (GINA). Strike it from intake templates.
  • Chart each element as performed or not. A template "normal" default records an exam that didn't happen.
  • Agility testing: the employer sets pass and fail; confirm it matches the real demand. With none set, report performance against the demand, with no pass or fail. If you stop a test for a medical concern, tell the employer only that it was stopped for a medical concern.
  • An injury during testing: treat, document, and notify the employer. Kansas: comp coverage turns on whether the applicant had entered a "contract of service."
  • Unrelated findings go to the applicant with a referral to their own clinician. They aren't treated here.
  • Kansas: the KAAD reaches employers with 4 or more employees (the ADA, 15), and the same post-offer rules apply. Pregnancy at this exam: see The pregnant worker.

Occupational vaccinations

Updated 2026-10-29

What it covers#

Immunity assessment (records or serology), vaccination, and documentation. Vaccines: hepatitis B, hepatitis A, influenza, MMR, varicella, Tdap or Td, and employer-mandated COVID-19. No travel vaccines.

ACIP governs every indication, schedule, and contraindication. Which ACIP recommendations are legally in effect is contested in 2026 (a March 2026 court stay is partly on appeal), so check at the time you give the vaccine.

The provider's role is clinical, not enforcing the employer's policy.

Hepatitis B under OSHA#

  • The employer offers the series at no cost within 10 working days of initial assignment to anyone with occupational blood exposure.
  • A worker may decline but signs the OSHA declination. They can change their mind later, still at no cost.
  • Don't restart an interrupted series. Continue where it left off.
  • Kansas: federal OSHA covers private employers only. Public employers, including fire, EMS, and police, aren't bound, and no Kansas rule replaces it.

Hepatitis B immunity#

  • A documented complete series and an anti-HBs of 10 mIU/mL or more means immune.
  • A titer of 10 or more without a documented series (and total core antibody not positive) is "immune by antibody testing," which meets the OSHA exemption. After an exposure, manage this worker as unvaccinated.
  • Check anti-HBs 1 to 2 months after the series. Below 10 isn't yet a non-responder: give one challenge dose and retest, or a second complete series. "Non-responder" applies only after two complete series, and there's no third series.
  • HBsAg positive: stop the series, refer to the worker's own clinician, and tell the employer only that the worker can't receive the vaccine for medical reasons. It isn't by itself a reason to exclude from work. Kansas: a new hepatitis B diagnosis is yours to report within 24 hours (see Reporting to KDHE).

Practice choice: a titer without a documented series

At the post-offer exam, a titer of 10 or more meets the OSHA exemption. After a blood exposure, a worker with no written, dated record of a complete series isn't considered immune, whatever the titer: the recommendation is the full series, or the signed Appendix A declination.

Practice choice: a low titer after one series

A low titer after one complete hepatitis B series gets a challenge dose and a retest. Still below 10: finish the second series and retest. Still below 10 after two complete series: test for HBsAg, and if it's negative, counsel the worker as a non-responder, who needs HBIG after any exposure.

Proof of immunity#

  • Proof that doesn't count: self-reported chickenpox (unless a provider diagnosed or verified it); measles, mumps, or rubella disease without lab confirmation; a dose with no written, dated record; last season's flu shot.
  • MMR and varicella for health care workers (ACIP): two documented doses, or lab evidence of immunity. Birth before 1980 doesn't count as evidence for varicella. At KU, two documented doses mean immune, and no titer is ordered.
  • Documented vaccination beats a later negative titer for MMR and varicella: no further dose, no retest. The exception: a woman of childbearing age whose rubella IgG isn't clearly positive gets one more MMR, with no retest.

Every dose#

  • Screen for pregnancy (by asking) and immunocompromise yourself before a live vaccine (MMR, varicella). Don't rely on the employer.
  • Give the current VIS (Vaccine Information Statement) before each dose.
  • Observe every recipient for 15 minutes, seated or lying, with epinephrine at hand.
  • Kansas: report every dose to KSWebIZ, the state registry, unless the person objects.
  • The employer gets status only: immune, series in progress, not immune, or declined, with dates. No titer values. Never tell the employer a contraindication or non-responder status.

Live vaccines

Two live vaccines (MMR, varicella) go on the same day, or at least 28 days apart. A live vaccine can also blunt a TB skin test or IGRA: test the same day as the vaccine, or wait 28 days after it. See TB screening and exposure and Vaccine timing.

Kansas mandates#

No Kansas statute requires occupational vaccination; one licensing rule does (birth-center staff exposed to blood need hepatitis B immunization or a documented refusal). An employer's COVID-19 requirement must exempt an employee with a physician-signed medical waiver or a religious waiver, at employers of any size, public included.

Drug and alcohol testing

Updated 2026-10-29

What the clinic does#

The clinic produces a properly collected specimen with an unbroken chain of custody. It never produces a drug test result. Trained MAs and technicians collect specimens and perform breath alcohol tests. Providers don't collect specimens or order drug screens.

Drug test results go from the lab to the MRO to the employer. They never come back through the clinic. If anyone asks "what did the test show?", the answer is always the MRO.

DOT and non-DOT#

  • DOT testing follows 49 CFR Part 40 exactly. FMCSA (commercial drivers) is the only DOT agency this clinic serves. A donor from FAA, FRA, FTA, PHMSA, or the Coast Guard raises a scope question before any collection. FRA (railroad) post-accident testing isn't a Part 40 collection at all; escalate, don't improvise.
  • Non-DOT testing follows the employer's policy and, where it applies, state law.
  • Never mix them. No non-DOT drugs on a DOT specimen, and no federal custody and control form (CCF) for a non-DOT test.
  • Return-to-duty and follow-up tests are always directly observed. The employer selects randoms; the clinic only collects.

The roles#

RoleWho
CollectorClinic MA or technician
BATBreath alcohol technician: clinic staff trained to run breath alcohol tests
MROMedical Review Officer: reviews lab results and interviews the donor. The clinic doesn't employ one.
DERThe employer's designated representative. The DER alone decides whether a refusal occurred.
SAP, C/TPASubstance abuse professional; consortium or third-party administrator. Outside the clinic.

Where the provider comes in#

  • Shy bladder, only when referred here. A donor who can't give 45 mL in 3 hours is sent by the DER, after consulting the MRO, for a physician evaluation within 5 days. You recommend to the MRO whether there's an ascertainable physiological condition or a documented pre-existing psychological disorder; situational anxiety or dehydration doesn't count. The MRO decides.
  • Escalations from a collection: a possible refusal, or disputed direct observation. Direct observation needs a specific Part 40 basis written on the CCF, never suspicion alone, and a same-sex observer.
  • Employer standing orders for an out-of-range temperature or tampering. Only the employer can authorize them.

Rules#

  • Treat an injured worker first. DOT (FMCSA) post-accident windows run from the accident: alcohol within 8 hours (with a written reason if not within 2), drugs within 32 hours.
  • Kansas post-accident tests (K.S.A. 44-501). For an employer's intoxication defense, the test must first be admissible, chiefly under a written testing policy in place before the injury. The specimen must then meet all six statutory conditions: collected within a reasonable time, by or under a licensed health care professional, tested by an HHS-certified or KDHE-licensed lab, GC-MS confirmation, chain of custody proven beyond a reasonable doubt, and a split sample available to the employee within 48 hours of a positive. Collect a non-DOT post-accident specimen with DOT discipline.
  • DOT donor ID (49 CFR 40.61(c)): a photo ID issued by the employer or a government, or identification by an employer representative who isn't a coworker. No faxes or photocopies. A donor without a photo ID isn't turned away if an employer representative can identify them. Without acceptable ID, the collector contacts the DER.
  • ID for every other visit or collection is in ID and registration.
  • Never tell a donor their DOT result, and never record a relayed result.
  • Don't record what a donor says about prescriptions or use. A donor with a prescription takes it to the MRO after the result.
  • No alcohol test before a job offer. Under the ADA it's a medical exam.
  • Marijuana: no medical explanation clears a DOT positive, and CBD is no defense. Kansas has no medical or recreational cannabis law, so a non-DOT employer can act on a positive.

Reasonable suspicion#

Under DOT, a trained supervisor's determination comes first. The signed written record may follow, within 24 hours of the observed behavior or before results are released, whichever is earlier. A collection site may require it in hand before collecting.

Practice choice: reasonable suspicion

A reasonable-suspicion test is collected on the trained supervisor's referral. The clinic doesn't wait for the signed written observation; it follows within the DOT deadline above. Waiting on it can miss the alcohol window.

Health care worker exams

Updated 2026-10-29

When this applies#

Post-offer and transfer exams for anyone who will work in a health care setting. How the visit runs in Net Health is in Employment exams. What's specific to TUKHS and UKP is in TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams. How long a prior result is accepted is in How long it's good for.

The components#

ComponentWhat the clinic does
Measles, mumps, rubellaTwo documented doses mean immune: no titer. Otherwise, order the titer.
VaricellaTwo documented doses mean immune: no titer. Otherwise, order the titer.
Hepatitis BCheck for documentation, but order the titer on everyone.
TBQFT or skin test. See TB screening and exposure.
Fit testWhen the job calls for one. See Respirator clearance.
  • Proof of immunity is written documentation or a titer result. Any record must carry two patient identifiers.
  • A prior fit test is accepted if it was within the past year on a mask the clinic has. If it's close to a year, do it again.

Low titers#

Low titerRecommended
Measles, mumps, or rubella, without two documented MMR dosesMMR until there are two documented doses, at least 28 days apart
Varicella, without two documented dosesVaricella vaccine until there are two documented doses, 4 to 8 weeks apart
Hepatitis B, after a documented complete seriesA challenge dose, then a retest
Hepatitis B, with no written, dated record of a complete seriesThe full series, as unvaccinated
Hepatitis B titer of 10 or more, with no documented seriesImmune for the post-offer exam. After a blood exposure, not immune: the full series, or the signed Appendix A declination.

The hepatitis B rows are practice choices; see Occupational vaccinations.

Vaccine timing#

  • Two live vaccines (MMR, varicella) go on the same day, or at least 28 days apart.
  • A live vaccine and a TB test go on the same day, or the test waits 28 days after the vaccine.
  • Inactivated vaccines (hepatitis B, influenza, Tdap) can go with any other vaccine, on any day.
  • Screen for pregnancy and immunocompromise before any live vaccine.

The pregnant worker

Updated 2026-10-28

The governing rule#

For a worker who is pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning a pregnancy. Each hazard's pregnancy limit is in that hazard's own note.

You answer the medical question and make a recommendation with its basis. The recommendation is made to the worker, and she decides. A restriction written over her objection on fetal risk alone is the sex-based exclusion Title VII forbids (Johnson Controls). A change she asks for is a PWFA accommodation question (see Return to work and fitness for duty).

At the post-offer exam#

Never

  • Pregnancy as a clearance factor
  • Asking whether she plans to become pregnant

Where the job carries a reproductive hazard, counsel every exposed worker, men included.

Exposures and vaccines#

  • At every exposure evaluation, ask about pregnancy and breastfeeding. The answer can change the prophylaxis offered.
  • Before live vaccines (MMR, varicella), settle pregnancy status by asking; routine testing isn't recommended. She avoids conception for 4 weeks after. If one is given in pregnancy by mistake, counsel her: registries found no congenital rubella or varicella syndrome. See Occupational vaccinations.
  • CMV and parvovirus B19: the occupational risk is in childcare and schools, not health care. CDC doesn't recommend routinely excluding pregnant health care workers from these patients; any change in work is her decision. Counsel hand hygiene and no shared food or utensils. Refer her to her obstetric provider if she has symptoms, and for parvovirus testing after a confirmed exposure. A positive CMV IgM alone doesn't mean new infection.
  • Hazardous drugs: the NIOSH list marks those hazardous in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and while trying to conceive. Several also affect men. The worker decides.

The injured pregnant worker#

Treat her like any worker, except:

  • Avoid NSAIDs from 20 weeks. Ask pregnancy status and gestational age before prescribing.
  • Don't withhold indicated imaging. An extremity film doesn't require checking pregnancy status, and shielding is no longer recommended.
  • After a blow to the abdomen, a fall, or a crash, a viable pregnancy warrants at least 4–6 hours of observation. If you can't monitor the fetus, send her somewhere that can.
  • When a wound needs a tetanus vaccine, give Tdap.

What the employer gets#

Document the exposure, the evidence, your recommendation and its basis, and her decision. The employer gets only the limitation, written against the named agent or task with its expected duration, and only if she wants it told.

Under the PWFA the employer may require only minimal documentation, and none for lactation, water, restroom breaks, sitting or standing, or breaks to eat.

Kansas: no state pregnancy-accommodation or lactation law; the federal PWFA and PUMP Act govern. Under the KAAD (4 or more employees), excluding someone for pregnancy is prima facie discrimination, and pregnancy disability is treated like any other temporary disability.

Industrial Safety

Ergonomics

Updated 2026-10-28

What it is#

Fitting the work to the worker. The risk factors are force, repetition, awkward or static posture, vibration, contact stress, and cold, most harmful in combination. The fix belongs at the workplace.

There's no federal ergonomics standard; OSHA cites ergonomic hazards under the General Duty Clause, and its industry guidelines are advisory. Kansas has no standard of its own.

Where you'll meet it#

  • At the post-offer exam, testing against the job's real demands (see Pre-placement exams).
  • At every treating visit. A strain or carpal tunnel case is also evidence about the job: record the load, frequency, posture, hours, and tools.
  • When you advise an employer, without a worker's diagnosis (see Industrial safety).

The same restriction for several workers from one task

The task is the problem.

What prevents injury#

  • Exercise has prevented back pain. Technique training and education alone haven't.
  • Back belts haven't prevented back pain, and pre-shift warm-ups have no evidence. A non-rigid back belt given in treatment is first aid; that says nothing about whether belts prevent injury.
  • For the upper extremity, workplace resistance training has the strongest evidence.

The NIOSH lifting equation#

It gives a recommended weight limit (RWL) for a two-handed lift: 51 lb under ideal conditions, reduced by six multipliers. The lifting index (LI) is the actual load divided by the RWL.

  • LI 1.0 or less is the design goal. Above 1.0, risk rises for some workers; above 3.0, for nearly all. The LI ranks jobs; it isn't one worker's risk.
  • Fix the smallest multiplier first. Remove the manual lift, then redesign the task, and only last split it between two workers.
  • It doesn't apply to one-handed, seated, or kneeling lifts, unstable loads, lifting mixed with much carrying, pushing, or pulling, or shifts over 8 hours. Don't average a multi-task job into one lift.
  • Pregnancy: NIOSH's provisional limits are lower than 51 lb. Lifting from below mid-shin and overhead have a limit of zero, and from 20 weeks the close-to-body zone isn't used. The advice is yours; the decision is hers (see The pregnant worker).
  • Patient handling: even for a cooperative patient lifted smoothly, the limit is 35 lb, less with arms extended, twisting, or kneeling. Above that, use equipment.

Line work#

Rotating between tasks that load the same tendons gives them no rest. New and returning workers carry the most risk in their first weeks, so don't start them at full line speed. Don't write a wrist splint for work when the job bends the wrist.

Industrial safety

Updated 2026-10-29

Two roles with one employer#
