The advisory role carries what the clinic sees in a workplace's injuries back to the employer as a fix: a site visit, an injury-pattern review, a safety talk. You can hold both roles with the same employer. Keep them apart.

TreatingAdvisory
You doRecord the exposure as reportedGive opinions on conditions and controls
You don'tRule on whether the employer's conditions were acceptableInclude a worker's diagnosis. Report clinic patterns in aggregate, with nothing that identifies a worker in a small department.

Only the workplace fact (a missing guard) and the control it points to cross between the roles.

Never sign a statement that a workplace is safe or compliant

The employer owns the program. You recommend and document; it decides and pays.

Controls#

  • Hierarchy, top down: elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE. Recommend the highest feasible control. A respirator clearance doesn't show the exposure is controlled.
  • A work restriction is an administrative control for one worker. The same restriction for several workers from one task means the task is the problem (see Ergonomics).
  • Exposure limits: "under the PEL" doesn't mean safe, and "below the TLV" doesn't mean compliant. The terms are in Exposure limits.
  • An industrial hygiene report: personal or area sample? Typical day? Full shift? It alone can't show one worker's illness came from that workplace. The worker, or a treating physician the worker designates in writing, may see the employer's exposure records.

The sentinel case#

Watch for:

  • a condition occupational almost by definition (occupational asthma, elevated blood lead)
  • more than one worker from one task with the same complaint
  • an injury from a missing or defeated control, or illness despite PPE
  • something new shortly before the cases began

Ask: is anyone else in this job having the same problem? and what changed?

Fatigue#

Fatigue belongs in the injury history: shift start, hours into the shift, hours worked the week before, consecutive nights, sleep before the shift, any second job, the commute.

Schedule restrictions need a diagnosis that calls for one, such as a seizure disorder provoked by sleep loss, or a diagnosed shift work sleep disorder that hasn't responded to treatment. Pregnancy is the exception: under the PWFA, a schedule change she asks for needs no diagnosis. Don't restrict her schedule on fetal risk when she hasn't asked (see The pregnant worker).

Kansas#

  • No state OSHA plan: federal OSHA covers private employers, not state and local government (see Kansas). No state exposure limits or workplace standards, except KDHE's radiation dose limits (see Radiation).
  • Point a small private employer to KDOL's free, confidential OSHA on-site consultation.
  • Most single occupational disease cases aren't reportable to KDHE. Blood lead and carbon monoxide poisoning are, and a cluster or unusual illness is a 4-hour report.

Other regulated operators

Updated 2026-10-28

Who decides#

Some jobs have a federal medical standard of their own. The regulator sets the criteria, and the regulator, or the employer it charges, makes the decision. You examine to its criteria and report what you found. Commercial drivers are in DOT certification; testing is in Drug and alcohol testing.

JobWho decidesKey point
Locomotive engineer, conductor (49 CFR 240/242)The railroad's medical examiner; the railroad certifiesVision, color vision, and hearing thresholds are in the rule
Merchant mariner (46 CFR 10, Subpart C)The Coast Guard, on form CG-719KA general exam for risk of sudden incapacitation, plus vision standards by credential
Pilot (14 CFR 67)An FAA-designated aviation medical examinerDon't issue the certificate unless you hold the designation. A pilot under 14 CFR 68 can be examined by any state-licensed physician.
Licensed reactor operator (10 CFR 55)The physician's determination; the plant certifies it to the NRC on Form 396An exam before licensing and every 2 years after
  • A missed threshold is usually not the end. Railroad workers can request further evaluation, be retested, and be certified with written restrictions. Mariners have Coast Guard waivers. The Federal Air Surgeon can grant a pilot a time-limited authorization or a statement of demonstrated ability. Record what the further evaluation will need.
  • A failed plate test is a screening result, not the decision. Don't report a color test the rule doesn't name as meeting the standard (for mariners, one the Coast Guard doesn't accept).
  • Railroad timing: the vision and hearing exam must be no more than 450 days old at the certification decision, and a certificate lasts no more than 36 months. The railroad, not the clinic, decides on an active substance-use disorder.

Cranes, forklifts, and heavy equipment#

No federal medical standard

Don't write a clearance against a medical standard that doesn't exist.

  • Without a regulator, a safety-sensitive exam is an individualized direct-threat assessment (see Pre-placement exams).
  • Match the exam to the machine: vision; color vision where signals or controls carry meaning; foot sensation where there are foot controls. Check depth perception only if the employer has a written requirement.
  • A crane certifier (NCCCO) requires the ASME B30 physical requirements, and accepts a DOT medical card as one way to show them in appropriate circumstances. The certifier or employer supplies the criteria.
  • Hours limits cap fatigue exposure but don't measure fatigue. A worker within every limit can still be impaired.
  • Kansas: OSHA's crane and forklift rules reach private employers, not state or local government. No Kansas license or medical requirement for crane operators was found; check with the city for any local license.

Bloodborne Pathogens

Bloodborne pathogen exposure

Updated 2026-10-29

What it is#

Urgent evaluation after a worker's exposure to someone else's blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM): a needlestick, a cut from a used sharp, or a splash to the eye, mouth, or broken skin. Intact skin isn't an exposure; if you can't tell, treat it as non-intact. The visit covers HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C.

The duties under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 fall on the employer; the written opinion is the provider's piece. Kansas public employers get the same care, but the standard isn't cited to them as binding (see Kansas).

Some workers arrive already on PEP from an ED. Count every time point from the exposure, not the visit.

For TUKHS staff asking about a source patient's results or next steps, see When to refer to Employee Health.

Time-critical

  • HIV PEP: start as soon as possible. The routine outer limit is 72 hours. Past 72 hours, a high-risk exposure still gets an expert consultation about starting: call PEPline.
  • Never hold the first dose for labs, the source result, a consultant, paperwork, insurance, or employer authorization.
  • HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin) ideally within 24 hours; 7 days is the outer limit.

The source#

The source is ordinarily tested where the exposure happened, and you request the result. Never test the needle.

Practice choice: the source patient isn't tested here

The source patient is tested where the exposure happened, never at this clinic.

Kansas: a health care, lab, EMS, fire, police, or corrections worker reports the exposure to the employer's infection control officer within 4 hours (K.A.R. 28-1-23). If the exposure could transmit infection, the infection control officer directs source testing alongside your care. A source who refuses testing needs a court order, which the agency head or infection control officer applies for, not you. None of this delays PEP.

Testing and follow-up#

  • The exposed worker is tested here at baseline.
  • Hepatitis B goes by documented vaccination and response. A dose without a written, dated record counts as not given, and a titer without a documented series doesn't make the worker immune after an exposure: recommend the full series, or the signed Appendix A declination. "Non-responder" means two failed series, not one.
  • Re-evaluate within 72 hours.
  • HIV: final test at 12 weeks. A 4–6 week test only if doses were missed or PEP started more than 24 hours after the exposure.
  • HCV: RNA at 3–6 weeks and antibody at 4–6 months, only when the source is HCV RNA-positive, antibody-positive with RNA unavailable, or unknown.
  • Book all of it before the worker leaves.

Call PEPline#

For no identifiable source, an undetectable source viral load, a worker on PrEP, and other complex cases. It isn't 24/7; the number and hours are in Phone numbers. After hours, use a local infectious disease or HIV expert.

Always ask about cabotegravir PrEP in the past 12 months. It adds a baseline NAT (nucleic acid test), and an expert sets the final test date.

What goes where#

  • The employer gets a limited written opinion: the worker was told the results, and was told of any condition needing more care. If the visit made a hepatitis B vaccination decision, a separate opinion says whether vaccination is indicated and whether it was given. No diagnoses or lab results. The employer must give the worker a copy within 15 days, so send the opinion promptly.
  • KDHE: a new HIV, HBV, or HCV diagnosis is reportable within 24 hours of lab evidence (routes in Reporting to KDHE). The exposure itself isn't.
  • The employer's logs: a contaminated sharps injury is recordable for an employer covered by OSHA recordkeeping. The clinic keeps neither the OSHA 300 log nor the sharps log; tell the employer so they can make the entries.
  • Records are kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years.
  • The worker pays nothing where the standard binds the employer: no copay, no deductible, whether or not a comp claim is filed or accepted.

DOT

DOT certification

Updated 2026-11-01

What it is#

A public-safety judgment, not a treatment visit. Can the driver safely operate a commercial motor vehicle? The controlling concern is sudden incapacitation at the wheel.

FMCSA sets the standard (49 CFR Part 391). The FMCSA Medical Examiner Handbook (January 2024) is guidance, but in practice it's the standard of care; document any departure. Only an examiner listed on the National Registry (NRCME) may perform the federal exam.

What this clinic adds is in DOT at this clinic. How the visit runs in Net Health is in DOT exams.

Outcomes and card length#

OutcomeNotes
Certify for the full periodUp to 24 months
Certify for a shorter periodCapped at 12 months: insulin-treated diabetes, the alternative vision standard, the exempt intracity zone, and a seizure exemption. Age 70 or older: a 1-year card is an option, not a rule.
Determination PendingUp to 45 days to get information
Not qualifiedComplete the exam even after you find a disqualifier
IncompleteThe driver leaves, or refuses to sign the certificate

The card expires at midnight on its date, with no grace period. Every visit is a complete exam, including a short-period recheck and the annual recertification for insulin or alternative vision.

Must-know rules#

  • Report every exam to the National Registry by midnight of the next calendar day, including incomplete exams and disqualifications. Foreign nationals are the exception (see Foreign nationals).
  • For CDL and permit holders, proof is the electronic state record, not the paper card (from October 12, 2026). FMCSA still recommends giving the driver a paper copy.
  • The certificate is all or nothing. No "daylight only" or "local routes only." Restrictions belong to the employer.
  • The carrier can't direct the outcome, length, or restrictions. Document any pressure and decline.
  • Determination Pending lets the driver keep driving on a current card. The conservative reading tells the driver that ends at day 45. If there's a real safety concern, disqualify instead.
  • No Determination Pending for a missing regulatory form. Without a valid MCSA-5870 (insulin-treated diabetes) or, for the alternative vision standard, a valid MCSA-5871, each signed within 45 days, there's no certificate that visit.
  • Blood pressure uses JNC-6 staging (140/90), not 2017 ACC/AHA. FMCSA's advisory criteria say don't certify at 180/110 or higher, whatever the history or treatment.
  • English proficiency isn't part of the medical determination (MCSA-5875 instructions). Examine only when you can communicate well enough to get a complete history; you may decline the exam when a language barrier prevents it (NRCME periodic training). FMCSA's ban on interpreters applies to the roadside and carrier English assessments, not the medical exam.
  • Noncitizen drivers: verify identity with a photo ID (a passport counts). Domicile doesn't matter to the examiner. Who may hold a non-domiciled CDL is the state licensing agency's question (FMCSA final rule, February 2026).
  • Specialist letters are information, not mandates. A "may return to work" note is not a DOT clearance.
  • Exemptions (seizure, hearing, and skill performance evaluation certificates for limb loss) come from FMCSA, never from the examiner, and are interstate-only. Vision and diabetes exemptions no longer exist; see Vision screening.

Hard disqualifiers

  • Marijuana in any form. A state card isn't a prescription.
  • Schedule I drugs
  • Antiseizure medication taken to prevent seizures, without an exemption
  • Severe non-proliferative or proliferative retinopathy in a driver on insulin

HbA1c alone never disqualifies. The urine dipstick is not a drug test; DOT drug testing is the employer's separate program.

What goes where#

  • The certificate (MCSA-5876): a non-CDL driver's goes to the carrier on request. A CDL or permit holder's goes only with consent.
  • The exam report (MCSA-5875) stays with the examiner. It goes to the employer only with the driver's consent.

Kansas variants#

  • Intrastate drivers are held to 49 CFR 391.41 (K.A.R. 82-4-3g). Check alternative-vision and insulin cases with the Kansas Corporation Commission (KCC), which also grants waivers. The Handbook says never complete both the federal and the state determination sections of the MCSA-5875.
  • School bus drivers (KSDE) get the same clinical standard before hire and at least every two years, on KSDE's own forms, with nothing filed to the National Registry. Any MD, DO, DC, PA, nurse practitioner, or registry examiner may do it. A driver on insulin goes the MCSA-5870 route (1-year card) or gets a KSDE board waiver. The card isn't the school certification of health, which a driver in regular contact with pupils also owes (see TB screening and exposure).
  • Fire apparatus operators usually aren't DOT drivers. A fire clearance never substitutes for a DOT card, and a DOT card never substitutes for a fire clearance.

DOT at this clinic

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

What this clinic does on top of the federal rules in DOT certification. How the visit runs in Net Health is in DOT exams. The driver's ID and license entry are in ID and registration.

Federal, not State#

Kansas adopts the federal regulations, so Kansas drivers get the Federal determination on the forms. The State determination isn't used here.

Drivers under 21

A common error is the State determination for a driver under 21. Use the Federal determination, as for any other driver.

Foreign nationals#

A foreign national is the exception to reporting every exam to the National Registry. The exam isn't uploaded to FMCSA; the driver gets the paper forms.

Interpreters#

Practice choice: interpreters

An interpreter can be used for a DOT exam. English proficiency is not part of the medical determination (see DOT certification).

Determination Pending#

Practice choice: Determination Pending

A driver on Determination Pending is told they may keep driving on the current card until day 45 or until that card expires, whichever comes first. Determination Pending doesn't extend the card.

Tools#

  • EasyDotExam.com https://www.easydotexam.com: DOT certification criteria by condition, for medical examiners.

Biological Exposures

TB screening and exposure

Updated 2026-10-29

The clinic's role#

Test, confirm latent TB infection with active disease ruled out, report, and refer. The clinic doesn't treat latent TB and doesn't manage active TB.

When you'll see it#

  • Baseline at hire for anyone working in a health care setting, paid or unpaid, not only clinical staff
  • After an exposure to an infectious patient without protection
  • Work rotations of a month or more with patient contact in high-incidence regions
  • Kansas school employees in regular contact with pupils need a signed certificate of health with a TB attestation (K.S.A. 72-6266). The statute names a negative skin test or a chest x-ray; whether a district accepts an IGRA is the district's call.
  • Kansas licensed facilities (hospitals, adult care homes, home health, child care, and others) set staff TB testing by their licensing rule. Check the facility's rule.

There's no routine annual testing after baseline without an exposure or ongoing transmission. A worker with untreated latent TB gets an annual symptom screen only. Where a state rule requires annual testing, it governs; ask the employer which rule applies and which test it accepts.

The test#

  • IGRA (blood test) is preferred. One visit, and BCG vaccination doesn't affect it.
  • A skin test (TST) is read at 48 to 72 hours in millimeters of induration, not redness. It's two-step at baseline.
  • Use the same test type at baseline and follow-up where you can.
  • A low-risk worker with a first positive at baseline is called infected only if a second test is also positive.
  • A live vaccine can blunt either test. See Occupational vaccinations.
  • How long a prior QFT, skin test, or chest x-ray is accepted is in How long it's good for. How QFT results are handled for TUKHS and UKP is in TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams.

After an exposure#

Test as soon as the exposure is identified, then again 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Never two-step after an exposure.

On a skin test, a worker whose prior test read 0 mm is positive at 5 mm or more, not 10.

Record the date of last exposure and both millimeter values. They're the evidence in a comp claim.

A positive test#

  • Symptom screen, a chest x-ray to rule out active TB, counseling, and referral for treatment.
  • Latent TB alone carries no work restriction. An asymptomatic worker works while the film is pending.
  • A positive second step on a two-step baseline is a boosted reaction (old infection), not a new conversion. It isn't a basis for a comp claim on its own, and the employer doesn't log it.
  • Kansas: report latent TB to KDHE within 24 hours of the positive skin test or IGRA, before the chest x-ray and before any confirmatory second test. Fax the form with the lab result. A worker tested in Kansas is reported to KDHE whatever the home state. See Reporting to KDHE.

Suspected active TB

Phone KDHE within 4 hours of suspicion, before any confirmation, then fax the form. Refer at once and exclude the worker from work. A negative IGRA or skin test doesn't rule it out. The number is in Phone numbers.

Vaccine-preventable disease exposures

Updated 2026-10-28

What it is#

A health care worker exposed to measles, chickenpox or shingles, pertussis, meningococcal disease, mumps, or rubella. One source case often exposes several workers.

  1. QualifyDoes the contact count as an exposure?
  2. ImmunityIs the worker immune?
  3. PEPIs post-exposure prophylaxis indicated, and inside what window?
  4. Monitor or excludeWhat monitoring or work exclusion applies?
  • Immunity matters for measles, chickenpox, mumps, and rubella only. It needs a dated vaccination record or a positive IgG. The worker's memory of the disease doesn't count, and neither does an MMR dose without a date. Pertussis and meningococcal disease are managed the same whatever the vaccine history.
  • If immunity is uncertain and the window is closing, give PEP. Don't wait for serology.
  • Meningococcal exposure is narrow: unprotected contact with secretions (mouth-to-mouth, intubation or suctioning without the right PPE), not being in the room.

PEP and work exclusion#

Windows count from the exposure, not the visit.

DiseasePEP and windowNon-immune worker off work
MeaslesMMR within 72 hours; immune globulin within 6 days (pregnant, can't take MMR, or severely immunocompromised)Day 5 after first exposure to day 21 after last, even with PEP
ChickenpoxVaccine within 5 days; VariZIG within 10 daysDay 8 to day 21; to day 28 if VariZIG given
PertussisAntibiotic as soon as possible, within 21 daysOnly if PEP is declined and the worker will see people at high risk of severe disease: kept from them 21 days
MeningococcalAntibiotic, ideally within 24 hours of identifying the index patientNone
MumpsNoneDay 10 to day 25
RubellaNoneDay 7 to day 23

Immune workers are monitored over the same window, not excluded.

An immune globulin referral isn't done until the receiving area has accepted the worker. State the exposure date and the deadline: a pregnant worker seen on day 4 after a measles exposure has two days, not six.

Pregnancy#

Live vaccines are contraindicated. A susceptible pregnant worker exposed to rubella is a priority case: serology, exclusion, and a prompt obstetrics consult. See The pregnant worker.

Kansas: reporting and notice#

The treating provider holds the reporting duty. Report even if infection control or the lab also reports.

ReportTiming
Measles, mumps, rubella, meningococcal disease, confirmed or suspectedPhone within 4 hours, then fax the form
Pertussis, chickenpoxFax within 24 hours, without waiting for labs
Any cluster or outbreakPhone within 4 hours

Shingles isn't reportable. Numbers and routes are in Reporting to KDHE.

The 4-hour notice (K.A.R. 28-1-23): an exposed health care, EMS, fire, police, or corrections worker reports to the employer's infection control officer within 4 hours. If you diagnose an airborne or droplet-spread disease in a patient who was transported to the facility, you notify the facility's infection control officer within 4 hours.

For TUKHS staff exposures, see also When to refer to Employee Health.

Rabies

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

  • Workers bitten or scratched by a possibly rabid animal, or whose eyes, mouth, or open wound met its saliva or nerve tissue
  • Pre-exposure vaccination (PrEP) for veterinary staff, animal control and wildlife officers, rabies lab workers, and cavers

Intact skin isn't an exposure. Petting, or saliva on intact skin, needs no post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).

Call KDHE for any potential exposure

The Epidemiology Hotline takes exposure calls 24/7; choose option 5 for a PEP consult (see Phone numbers). The PEP decision is made with the health department, never alone. If it recommends PEP, start it.

Care#

  • Wound care first: soap and water, thoroughly. Avoid primary suturing if you can. Check tetanus.
  • PEP is a medical urgency, not an emergency. There's time to consult, but don't wait days on animal testing for a high-risk animal. There's no absolute time limit: if the worker has no signs of rabies, start PEP whatever the interval. A negative test on the animal is grounds to stop.
  • Animal risk: bats are highest. A bat in the room of someone who was asleep may warrant PEP; call, don't dismiss it. Skunks, raccoons, foxes, and coyotes are high risk.
  • Pregnancy doesn't change PEP.

HRIG#

  • An unvaccinated worker gets HRIG with the first vaccine dose. Never give HRIG to a previously vaccinated worker.
  • Check stock against the weight-based dose. Without enough, transfer the worker the same day. If same-day transfer can't happen, give the first vaccine dose and get HRIG by day 7. A series started without HRIG still gets it up to day 7, never after.
  • HRIG never goes in the same syringe or site as the vaccine. Vaccine goes in the deltoid, never the buttock.
  • A series started elsewhere: get the records, count from the true day 0, and don't repeat HRIG.

Practice choice: HRIG on hand

The clinic stocks HRIG.

Pre-exposure titers#

PrEP titers can't answer an acute exposure question. Boost below 0.5 IU/mL. Kansas State's lab reports print a 0.1 IU/mL line beside 0.5; read every result against 0.5.

The animal#

A biting owned dog, cat, or ferret is observed for 10 days, whatever its vaccination status, with no PEP unless it shows signs of rabies. A biting stray or unwanted one is euthanized and tested at once at the Kansas State University Rabies Laboratory.

Kansas: the reservoirs are skunks and bats, and rabid cats have been reported. A county with no positive animals may just have few submissions. A potential exposure isn't legally reportable; the call to KDHE is the clinical standard. A suspected human rabies case is a 4-hour phone report.

Workers' comp#

PEP can cost several thousand dollars. Coverage depends on the first-visit record of the exposure, the animal, and the worker's duties, so document all three.

Zoonoses and tick-borne infection

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

  • Outdoor workers with tick-borne disease: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, Lyme, alpha-gal syndrome
  • Workers who handle animals, birds, tissues, birth products, urine, or droppings: tularemia, Q fever, brucellosis, leptospirosis, hantavirus, avian influenza (H5N1), psittacosis

Rabies is in Rabies.

Kansas: tularemia is common here, mostly May to September, from ticks, deer flies, cat bites, and mowing near sick or dead animals. Ehrlichiosis is the most common tick-borne disease. Alpha-gal syndrome occurs here.

The history makes the diagnosis#

The worker won't mention the exposure unless asked. Ask every febrile worker about ticks, animals and birds (birthing, slaughter, necropsy, raw milk), cleaning a closed rodent-infested building, water or animal urine, lab work, and travel. Only 55–60% of RMSF patients remember a tick bite.

Treat on suspicion

RMSF, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, tularemia, Q fever, and leptospirosis test negative early. A negative test in the first week decides nothing. Doxycycline for RMSF is recommended at every age and in pregnancy; don't delay it for a consult.

PresentationThinkDo
Fever and headache in an outdoor worker in tick season, no rash yetRMSFDoxycycline that day
Flu-like illness weeks after cleaning a barn, shed, or vacant buildingHantavirusED that day
Febrile livestock worker with a valve problem, graft, or aneurysm, or who is pregnantQ fever (chronic endocarditis risk)Treat; flag the risk at the first visit
Febrile lab or animal-care worker after a culture, necropsy, or birthTularemia or brucellosisWarn the lab before it handles the specimen

Tick bite#

  • Don't test the tick, or a worker with no symptoms.
  • No antibiotic prevents the rickettsial diseases. Single-dose doxycycline is for Lyme risk only, within 72 hours of removal, when CDC's criteria are met.
  • Return for fever, rash, or headache within 2 weeks.

Avian influenza (H5N1)#

Think of it in a dairy or poultry worker with conjunctivitis. A sick exposed worker gets standard, contact, and airborne precautions plus eye protection, H5 testing through KDHE's state lab, and oseltamivir without waiting for results. The worker stays out of work until H5 is ruled out. After an unprotected high-risk exposure, prophylaxis is considered, at the twice-daily treatment dose.

Pregnancy#

Acute toxoplasmosis in a pregnant worker goes to obstetrics and infectious disease at once. See The pregnant worker.

Reporting to KDHE#

ReportTiming
Suspected novel influenza A, including H5N1Phone within 4 hours
Hantavirus, every suspected caseWithin 24 hours
Suspected tularemiaWithin 24 hours (KDHE asks for it)
Tularemia, brucellosis, and lab exposures to either; Q fever, leptospirosis, spotted fever, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, Lyme, psittacosisWithin 24 hours of lab evidence

Numbers and routes are in Reporting to KDHE.

Environmental Exposures

Chemical exposures

Updated 2026-10-29

Most stay, most go back to work#

Most chemically exposed workers stay in the clinic, and most return to work the same day. For a worker with no symptoms, creating a record is a legitimate reason for the visit.

First minutes#

  1. IrrigateBurns and splashes: irrigate first, then assess. Use plenty of water, and never neutralize.
  2. Identify the agentA trade name isn't an agent. Ask for the SDS (safety data sheet) every time. In a medical emergency, a "proprietary" ingredient must be disclosed to you at once.
  3. Call Poison Controlwhen irrigation starts if you need the agent's irrigation endpoint, or at the start of the visit if the agent's category is unclear (see Phone numbers).
  4. Keep or send outDecide by the agent's category, not by how the worker looks.

These go out, even if the worker looks well

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors (organophosphates, carbamates). Act on the toxidrome; don't wait for the SDS.
  • Chemical asphyxiants: carbon monoxide (including from methylene chloride, hours later), methemoglobin formers, hydrogen sulfide, cyanide, arsine. Pulse oximetry can't detect carboxyhemoglobin or methemoglobin.
  • Hydrofluoric acid and other agents absorbed through the skin (phenol, aniline). For hydrofluoric acid, pain out of proportion to the mark is the clue.
  • Irritant gases with delayed lung injury: nitrogen dioxide (silo gas), phosgene, ozone, metal fumes such as cadmium. A normal first lung exam is expected.
  • Any unidentified agent from a confined space, especially if the worker was found down or lost consciousness.
  • Contamination the clinic can't remove without contaminating itself.

Disposition is binary: home with agent-specific return precautions, or transfer. There's no observation hold in clinic. A transferred worker doesn't drive.

Decontamination#

Don't walk a contaminated worker through the waiting room. "Decontaminated" is a conclusion, not a finding. Remove clothing, brush off powder, irrigate with water.

Radiological: an exposed worker isn't radioactive. Without a survey meter the clinic can't verify decontamination, so a contaminated worker is transferred. Treat injuries first. See Radiation.

Practice choice: no decontamination here

The clinic is not a decontamination facility.

Practice choice: calcium gluconate gel on hand

The clinic stocks 2.5% calcium gluconate gel. For hydrofluoric acid on the skin, irrigate, apply the gel, and send the worker out with it.

Pitfalls#

  • Alkali keeps penetrating, so after prolonged contact re-evaluation is mandatory. Wet cement is the burn most often kept and misjudged: little or no pain at first, and a single shift can produce a full-thickness injury.
  • A urine drug screen is not a toxicology panel. A cholinesterase level in a worker with no symptoms means nothing without a baseline.
  • Don't write a precautionary restriction. It reaches the worker's pay and can make the case recordable. A sensitized worker's restriction names the agent, with no dose. In pregnancy, a recommendation to avoid the agent is made to the worker, and she decides.
  • Recordkeeping: irrigation is first aid. A prescription or any loss of consciousness makes the case recordable.
  • Don't use the word "overexposure," and give no opinion on the employer's ventilation or PPE.

Kansas#

Report carbon monoxide poisoning to KDHE within 24 hours, on suspicion. Acute pesticide illness isn't reportable. Whether a single release is an accident or an occupational disease is unsettled, so record the agent, date, time, place, shift, and symptom onset.

Lung disease and damp buildings

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

New or worse asthma, recurrent flu-like illness after shifts, and workers sick from one building. No OSHA standard covers occupational asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, organic dust, or damp buildings, and there's no exposure limit for mold. Acute inhalation injury is in Chemical exposures.

History#

  • Ask every adult with new or worsening asthma about work.
  • Ask about weekends. Improvement can take days, so it may show only on a holiday.
  • An isocyanate worker may have only evening cough, 4–8 hours after exposure.
  • Record two dates: the last exposure, and the first day the worker couldn't do the job.

Work-related asthma#

TypeRestriction
Sensitizer-inducedRemoval from the agent. Name the agent and write no dose.
Irritant-induced (including RADS) or work-exacerbatedReduced exposure. A level can be written.
  • Confirm it objectively while the worker is still exposed; history alone was wrong in about a quarter of suspected cases. Serial peak flow: at least four readings a day, for at least two weeks at work and two off.
  • Unless it's unsafe, the worker stays in the job until tested. A moved worker can't do serial peak flow at the exposure.
  • One sensitized worker is a sentinel event.

The diagnosis not to miss: hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Recurrent flu-like illness hours after a shift, or months of worsening breathlessness, dry cough, and weight loss with bibasilar crackles and no wheeze. At the visit where you suspect it, advise stopping the exposure and refer to pulmonology.

Organic dust toxic syndrome is fever 4–12 hours after heavy moldy-dust exposure, often in most of a crew, settling within days. If crackles, imaging, or lung function point past a self-limited illness, or episodes keep recurring, treat it as hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

The damp building#

  • Whether a building is safe is an industrial-hygiene question, not a clinical one (see Exposure limits). A spore count can't show compliance.
  • No mycotoxin panels. "Toxic mold syndrome" and CIRS aren't recorded as diagnoses.
  • Decline without dismissing. Say first that the symptoms are taken seriously, then why the test won't help.
  • An outside "mold toxicity" diagnosis is neither adopted nor rebutted. Document your own findings.
  • Several sick workers from one space make a building cause more likely. Recommend an independent building assessment, and still evaluate each worker on their own findings.
  • Restrictions are written by place ("no work in Building C"). Return needs confirmed remediation.

Infections not to miss#

  • Pneumonia not clearing on antibiotics after disturbing soil or droppings: histoplasmosis or blastomycosis. Start with a urine antigen.
  • Pneumonia around water mist (cooling towers, plumbing): Legionnaires'. Treat without waiting. Send a urinary antigen (serogroup 1 only) and a lower-respiratory culture or molecular test.

Kansas#

  • KDHE: histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and legionellosis within 24 hours of lab evidence. A single case of blastomycosis, pneumoconiosis, or damp-building illness isn't reported.
  • A cluster of occupational lung disease is a 4-hour phone report. Whether KDHE expects a damp-building cluster reported is KDHE's call: phone the Epidemiology Hotline and ask (see Reporting to KDHE).
  • Damp-building illness is an occupational disease under comp. Work-relatedness for a claim is the adjudicator's decision.

Heat and cold

Updated 2026-10-28

No heat standard#

There's no final federal heat standard and no Kansas one. NIOSH guidance is recommendation, not obligation.

Heat#

Triage first: is mental status normal? Check it at the door. An escort saying "he's not himself" counts as abnormal.

Heat stroke: cool first, transport second

Any CNS dysfunction in a hot, exerting worker.

  • Start cooling at recognition, even in the parking lot. Call EMS in parallel, and keep cooling through handoff.
  • Strip, wet the skin with the coldest water available, and fan hard. Without a rectal temperature, cool until mental status, heart rate, and blood pressure are normal.
  • Sweating doesn't exclude it. Only a rectal temperature is reliable.
  • Treat every heat stroke as rhabdomyolysis until labs say otherwise. Dark urine after hot work is not dehydration to send home.
  • Heat syncope is evaluated as syncope. Consider cardiac causes first.
  • Exertional hyponatremia (a lot of plain water over a long shift) looks like heat exhaustion, and heat-exhaustion treatment harms it. With neurological findings, send out for a sodium.

Back to work after heat illness#

  • After heat exhaustion: depending on the hour, off the rest of the day, then full duty the next. The first shift is best at a reduced pace through the hottest hours, as a recommendation, not a restriction. No restriction for a resolved event.
  • After heat stroke: at least a week out of exertion after release from care, then the new-worker ramp over 2 to 4 weeks, with a buddy and no working alone. Refer if not progressing by 4 to 6 weeks.
  • Acclimatization is lost after a week or more away. NIOSH's ramp: new workers start at no more than about 20% of full heat time and add no more than about 20% a day; returning experienced workers start at 50%.
  • Write heat restrictions by exposure condition (time in heat, impermeable PPE), never by job title such as "no outdoor work." Make them temporary; a permanent one is a fitness-for-duty question.
  • Medications and obesity are risk factors, not grounds for restriction. Ask about pregnancy directly; a recommendation to leave hot work is made to her, and she decides.

Cold#

  • Frostbite: rewarm only if the part can be kept thawed. Thawing and refreezing is worse than staying frozen. No rubbing or dry heat: water at 37 to 39 °C (98.6 to 102.2 °F), with analgesia. Deep injury, hemorrhagic blisters, and whole- or multi-digit injury go out the same day.
  • Non-freezing cold injury (wet boots all shift) is missed when the only complaint is feet that hurt after rewarming. Rewarm gradually, without immersion. Dry footwear is a condition of return.
  • Hypothermia: a shivering, mildly confused worker is mild and can be rewarmed in clinic. A worker who has stopped shivering, is markedly confused or drowsy, or has a depressed level of consciousness is an emergency and goes out.

Clusters#

Two workers from one crew on one shift is a cluster. Tell the employer the pattern factually, without judging its controls.

Kansas: heat illness and cold injury aren't reportable to KDHE, but a cluster is a 4-hour phone report under the general cluster rule (K.A.R. 28-1-2(b)).

Skin disease

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

Mostly hand dermatitis from wet work, gloves, and sensitizers, plus contact urticaria and latex. Chemical burns, including wet cement, are in Chemical exposures.

Treat a hand rash in a working adult as possibly occupational until the history says otherwise. There's no OSHA skin standard; the employer selects and requires gloves.

Irritant or allergic?#

The first question, because the two carry different restrictions.

IrritantAllergic
What it isDose-dependent barrier injury; atopic dermatitis is the biggest personal riskLifelong sensitization, possibly after years of tolerance
The restriction namesThe exposure condition (time in wet work, glove time with a liner)The allergen, with no dose
UsuallyManaged in the jobAvoidance only

Patch testing is the only way to tell them apart and name the allergen. Refer to dermatology or allergy when the rash hasn't improved 3 months after advice and exposure changes, allergy is suspected, or the diagnosis would change the worker's job. Send the product list, SDSs, photos, and your question.

The visit#

  • History: each task, every product by name with its SDS, glove type and wear time, hand washes per shift, the course over weekends and vacations, home exposures, atopy, coworkers affected.
  • Examine all the skin, not just the hands. Take dated photos before treatment.
  • Scrape before you prescribe a steroid. Tinea of one hand is the mimic to rule out.
  • Better on days off raises suspicion but doesn't confirm a work cause. Use Mathias's seven criteria: four or more supports probable occupational causation. Record each answer.
  • Treatment: reduce the exposure first. Emollients, alcohol rub instead of soap where hygiene allows, a site-matched topical steroid. Don't promote barrier creams as protection.
  • Latex: a delayed allergy to rubber accelerators is a rash, and nitrile carries the same accelerators. Only immediate latex-protein allergy (hives under the glove, rhinitis, wheeze) reaches the airway.
  • The prognosis is poor: about 1 in 5 report complete healing 4–5 years later. Early diagnosis changes the course.

Recognize

  • Chrome ulcer: painless, punched-out, on a finger web, knuckle, or nasal septum in a plating, tanning, or cement worker. Heal it, identify the exposure, and raise chromium surveillance with the employer (see Other metals).
  • Chloracne: refer.
  • A non-healing or changing lesion in an outdoor, tar-, or oil-exposed worker: biopsy.

Records and reporting#

  • A prescription-strength steroid makes the case recordable. Don't comment on the employer's glove program either way.
  • At a pre-placement exam, past dermatitis is counseling, not exclusion.
  • Kansas: skin disease isn't reportable to KDHE; a cluster is a 4-hour phone report. A wet-work dermatosis is an occupational disease under comp. The carrier or adjudicator decides compensability; you document the facts.

Pressure and altitude

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

Most divers you'll see aren't commercial: fire and sheriff dive teams, instructors, research divers, hyperbaric chamber attendants. Also workers sent to altitude.

The exam won't show the exposure, so ask: were you under pressure, or at altitude, in the last day? A diver with shoulder pain reports a shoulder; a chamber attendant presents as a nurse.

Cases not to miss

  • Joint pain, numbness, or fatigue in the day after a dive or chamber shift: decompression sickness until excluded. Most start within an hour of surfacing, nearly all within six.
  • Collapse or stroke-like signs within minutes of surfacing: arterial gas embolism, even after a shallow dive.
  • Unwell after the flight home or a drive over a mountain pass: the worker has decompressed a second time.
  • A headache worse on the second day at altitude: acute mountain sickness. Ataxia (use the heel-to-toe walk) or a change in mental status is high-altitude cerebral edema: descend now.
  • Breathlessness out of proportion to effort, with a dry cough, at altitude: early high-altitude pulmonary edema, even with a clear chest.

Treatment#

  • Decompression illness: 100% oxygen, lie flat (no head-down tilt), transfer to a chamber. Don't hold for a chest film. Symptoms that resolve on oxygen can return. Calling a case "mild" is the diving physician's decision, not yours.
  • Vertigo or hearing loss after a hard descent may be inner-ear barotrauma rather than decompression sickness. Refer the same day either way, and record which you suspected and why.
  • At altitude, descent is the treatment. A worker with cerebral edema doesn't descend alone.

Fitness exams#

  • Examine to a named standard, and the record says which. No federal rule requires an exam for public-safety, instructional, or research divers. Follow what the department or certifying body names, such as NFPA 1580 for a fire dive team (see Fire and law enforcement).
  • The one federal rule requiring a physician is compressed-air construction (29 CFR 1926.803): before first exposure, after 10 days' absence or any absence for illness or injury, and at least yearly.
  • Histories that change the answer: spontaneous pneumothorax (barred, even after pleurodesis, with one narrow exception), epilepsy, insulin-treated diabetes, pregnancy, an open eardrum perforation. A childhood febrile seizure or an oxygen-toxicity seizure isn't epilepsy.
  • Altitude clearance names a destination altitude and ascent schedule, never "cleared for altitude." Restrictions name the exposure ("no hyperbaric exposure until…"), not the job.

Kansas#

Public fire and police dive teams are outside federal OSHA, and no Kansas rule sets a medical standard for them; the department's own standard governs. Decompression and altitude illness aren't reportable to KDHE; a cluster is a 4-hour phone report.

Radiation

Updated 2026-10-28

Who comes in#

Imaging and nuclear-medicine staff (the largest group), industrial radiographers, gauge and well-logging technicians. Also laser, UV, radiofrequency, and MRI exposures.

No federal rule requires a medical exam of a radiation worker. Monitoring, records, and reports belong to the employer. An employer-requested exam follows the employer's program, and the record says which.

Three ideas#

  • A badge dose is a regulatory number, not a lab result. A dose at or near the annual limit causes no symptom or finding. Injury takes ten times that or more, delivered in minutes.
  • Exposure isn't contamination. A worker exposed to a beam or sealed source is no hazard. A contaminated worker is handled as a chemical exposure (see Chemical exposures) and, without a survey instrument, sent elsewhere.
  • Don't estimate a dose in the clinic. The employer's radiation safety officer reconstructs it.

Cases not to miss

  • Nausea and vomiting after a day near a source: possibly the start of acute radiation syndrome. Feeling fine the next morning is the latent stage, not recovery.
  • A radiographer with a reddened finger or hand and no burn mechanism: a handled or pocketed source. A non-healing ulcer follows.
  • Bilateral eye pain the night after a shift: photokeratitis (see Eye injury). A scotoma after a laser exposure goes to ophthalmology the same day, with the laser's class and wavelength from its label.
  • A flameless burn in a tower or antenna worker may be radiofrequency.
  • MRI-suite workers need the implant questions. The field is on even when the scanner is idle.

The visit#

  • Make two calls: the employer's radiation safety officer, at the start of the visit, and REAC/TS at Oak Ridge (24 hours; after hours 865-576-1005).
  • The blood count is a curve. Draw a CBC with differential at the visit, recording the exposure and draw times. Where whole-body exposure is possible, repeat on CDC's serial schedule. A single normal count excludes nothing.
  • Who leaves: a possible whole-body dose in the acute-radiation-syndrome range goes to the ED with the first CBC drawn. A suspected local injury is referred for weeks of follow-up. An anomalous badge with no credible exposure stays.
  • No restriction is written to keep an overexposed worker from more dose; the licensee's limit does that.
  • Pregnancy: the fetal limit (0.5 rem for the pregnancy) applies only if she declares in writing. Declaring is voluntary and can be withdrawn. Your job is to explain the choice.

Kansas#

  • Kansas is an NRC Agreement State, so Kansas's own dose limits and rules apply. The licensee, not the clinic, reports an overexposure to KDHE.
  • Occupational-disease time limits don't apply to ionizing radiation; a cancer decades later isn't barred by them.
  • A Department of Energy or atomic-weapons-site worker with cancer may also qualify for federal EEOICPA compensation. Point them to it.

Medical Surveillance

Lead

Updated 2026-10-29

How surveillance works#

Lead, asbestos, silica, other metals, and HAZWOPER share a pattern. First decide which standard applies, general industry or construction; that sets who's covered, the schedule, and the timelines. The employer measures exposure and decides who's covered. The provider runs the surveillance and writes an opinion with the required elements. What the employer may be told differs by program (see What leaves the building). Respirator clearance is a separate evaluation, often done at the same visit (see Respirator clearance).

Federal OSHA doesn't cover state and local government employers, and Kansas has no state plan. HAZWOPER alone reaches a public hazmat team, through an EPA rule.

Who's covered#

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1025 (general industry) and 1926.62 (construction).

  • General industry: at or above the action level (30 µg/m³ of air) for more than 30 days a year.
  • Construction: a blood lead and ZPP after any single day at or above the action level; the full program after more than 30 days in any 12 months.

Blood lead schedule#

  • Last blood lead below 40 µg/dL: every 6 months. Construction: every 2 months for the first 6 months, then every 6.
  • Last blood lead 40 or more: every 2 months until two in a row are below 40.
  • Under removal: monthly.
  • Kansas: report every blood lead result to KDHE within 24 hours, whatever the value.
  • Ask about non-work lead at every visit: shooting and reloading, renovating pre-1978 homes, folk remedies.

Medical removal#

  • General industry has two triggers. Don't watch only for 60. Remove at a confirmed blood lead of 60 or more, or when the average of the last three tests is 50 or more (unless the latest is below 40). Construction: a confirmed 50 or more.
  • Confirm within 2 weeks. Don't wait for confirmation with encephalopathy, severe symptoms, or a blood lead above 100.
  • Return after two consecutive results below 40.
  • A final medical determination makes removal mandatory at any blood lead when it finds a medical condition that places the worker at increased risk from lead. In construction, that determination is the examining physician's written opinion (1926.62(k)(1)(ii)(B)). In general industry, it's the outcome of multiple physician review or an agreed alternate mechanism (1910.1025(k)(1)(ii)(B)).
  • Write it as removal from exposure, not from work. The employer protects a removed worker's earnings and seniority for up to 18 months; that's the employer's duty.
  • No chelation to get a worker back to work. Prophylactic chelation is prohibited.
  • Verify thresholds at osha.gov/lead before any removal decision. OSHA's threshold rulemaking has stalled.

Below OSHA's thresholds, ACOEM (2023) recommends removal at two results of 20 or more taken 4 weeks apart, or a single result of 30 or more, with return below 15. These are recommendations, not law. If you recommend removal on this basis, document the basis and each party's response. The employer may decline. If it does remove the worker because of the blood lead or its effects, OSHA requires the same protection of earnings and seniority, for at least 18 months, as for a removal the standard requires. The Review Commission has held that an elevated blood lead below the triggers counts as a medical condition for this purpose.

Practice choice: ACOEM 2023 counseling

Counseling follows ACOEM's 2023 recommendations.

Practice choice: removal below OSHA's thresholds

Removal from exposure is recommended below OSHA's thresholds, per ACOEM. It's written as a recommendation, not as a final medical determination that would make removal mandatory.

Pregnancy: ACOEM advises avoiding exposure that would raise blood lead above 3.5 µg/dL. Recommend with your reasons; the decision is hers. See The pregnant worker.

The written opinion#

It includes the blood lead results. Only findings unrelated to lead are withheld from the employer.

The second opinion

When the employer chose the examining physician, the worker may seek a second physician's review. The employer can make its participation and payment conditional on the worker giving notice and starting to book it within 15 days. State the deadline whenever you state the right, in a cover letter, not the opinion.

Kansas comp#

A disease from exposure, with no trauma behind it, is decided on the separate occupational-disease track (K.S.A. 44-5a01). The employer is liable only if disablement comes within one year of the last injurious exposure.

Asbestos

Updated 2026-10-28

Which standard#

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1001 (general industry) and 1926.1101 (construction). In the Kansas City metro, construction is the common one, from renovation and abatement work. The two aren't interchangeable, so establish which applies before you apply any schedule. There's no action level; surveillance is keyed to the exposure limit itself. The surveillance pattern is in How surveillance works.

General industryConstruction
Who's coveredAnyone exposed at or above the exposure limit, with no 30-day floorA combined 30 or more days a year of Class I–III asbestos work or exposure at or above a limit
First examBefore assignmentWithin 10 working days after the 30th day
Periodic examAt least annuallyAt least annually
Chest x-rayA fixed schedule by age and years since first exposure, every 1 to 5 yearsAt the examining physician's discretion
Termination examWithin 30 days before or after terminationNone

The exam is annual; only the x-ray is spaced out.

Not every respirator wearer belongs in the program. A construction worker in a negative-pressure respirator who doesn't reach 30 days is owed a determination that they can do the work and wear the respirator, not the full surveillance exam.

How the visit runs in Net Health is in Respirator exams.

The exam#

  • The respiratory questionnaire (Appendix D) is required: Part 1 at the first exam, Part 2 at periodic exams. Without it the exam is incomplete.
  • The film is read with the ILO system by a B reader, a board-eligible or certified radiologist, or a physician with known expertise in pneumoconioses.
  • Spirometry: a non-physician who runs it must have completed a spirometry training course. Normal spirometry doesn't clear a worker whose film is abnormal.
  • The result isn't "cleared" or "not cleared." Identify risk conditions, recommend PPE, refer, and document.
  • Pleural plaques mark past exposure. They aren't premalignant and aren't by themselves a reason for restriction.

Practice choice: who reads the chest film

Chest films are read by a B reader or a board-certified radiologist.

Act now, not next cycle

Weight loss, night sweats, or new pleuritic pain.

The written opinion#

The employer gets the exam results and four statements, and nothing unrelated to asbestos:

  1. Whether further exposure increases the worker's risk
  2. Any recommended limits on the worker or on protective equipment, respirators included
  3. That the worker was told the results and any asbestos-related condition needing further explanation or treatment
  4. That the worker was told of the added lung cancer risk from smoking combined with asbestos. This is the one that gets dropped. It's owed to every worker, smoker or not.

Silica's privacy rule is stricter. Don't carry one program's habit into the other.

Kansas#

Asbestosis isn't reportable to KDHE. Mesothelioma goes to the Kansas Cancer Registry within six months of diagnosis. Asbestos disease claims run on the separate occupational-disease track (K.S.A. 44-5a01).

Silica

Updated 2026-10-28

Which standard#

OSHA's 2016 standards: 29 CFR 1910.1053 (general industry) and 1926.1153 (construction). The triggers catch different workers, so confirm which governs before deciding surveillance is owed. The surveillance pattern is in How surveillance works.

General industryConstruction
TriggerAt or above the action level (25 µg/m³) for 30 or more days a yearRequired to wear a respirator 30 or more days a year. Under OSHA's enforcement directive, any part of a day counts as a full day, and the count is per employer.
ExamsWithin 30 days of assignment, then at least every 3 yearsSame

More frequent exams are at the examiner's recommendation. No transfer or diagnosis-triggered exam is required; don't tell an employer one is.

Engineered-stone countertop fabricators get accelerated, early-onset disease. Five years into the trade with new dyspnea isn't too early for silicosis.

The exam#

  • Latent TB testing is required at baseline only. Repeat testing is often warranted on individual risk but isn't an OSHA requirement. The standard names no test; IGRA is generally preferred (see TB screening and exposure). Take a TB history at every visit, and rule out active TB before treating a positive result.
  • The x-ray is read by a NIOSH-certified B reader, with the ILO system.
  • The spirometry technician needs a current certificate from a NIOSH-approved course.
  • A B read of 1/0 or higher makes a specialist recommendation mandatory. The specialist is board-certified in pulmonary disease or occupational medicine. With authorization, the employer must make that exam available within 30 days.
  • Normal spirometry doesn't rule out silicosis. The radiograph is the diagnostic test.
  • No removal threshold. Recommending removal from exposure is your clinical judgment, and it reaches the employer only with authorization.

Evaluate now

Fever, weight loss, night sweats, or hemoptysis may mean TB, another mycobacterial infection, or lung cancer.

Two written products, each within 30 days#

  • To the worker: the full results, any respirator or exposure limits, and a specialist recommendation where it applies. Explain the results to the worker directly.
  • To the employer: only the exam date, a statement that the exam met the standard, and any respirator limitations. Exposure limits and a specialist referral are added only with the worker's written authorization.

Counsel the worker on authorization. Without it, the employer never learns a specialist is recommended, can't arrange the visit, and doesn't have to pay for it. Document the discussion.

The strictest privacy rule of the three

Never send diagnoses, x-ray findings, spirometry, or TB results to the employer. A habit carried over from lead or asbestos will breach it.

Kansas#

Silicosis isn't reportable to KDHE. Claims run on the separate occupational-disease track (K.S.A. 44-5a01), with time limits counted from the last injurious exposure; for death, silicosis alone has three years instead of one.

Other metals

Updated 2026-10-28

Four standards, one shape#

Chromium (VI), cadmium, beryllium, and inorganic arsenic each have an OSHA standard built like lead's (see How surveillance works). An air action level switches on surveillance. The employer measures it, counts the days, and must send you a packet that includes prior exams (for beryllium, prior exams only with the worker's written consent).

The day counts differ: chromium is owed at or above the action level 30 or more days a year, beryllium more than 30, arsenic only above the action level. Construction cadmium also covers listed tasks, such as cadmium brazing, whatever the air level.

Periodic examBiological monitoringWhat the employer getsRemoval
Chromium (VI)AnnualNone requiredOpinion within 30 daysNone
CadmiumWithin 1 year, then at least every 2; labs at least yearlyUrine and blood cadmium, urine β2-microglobulinThe diagnosis and the absorption resultsMandatory at triggers; pay protected up to 18 months
BerylliumEvery 2 yearsBeLPTA closed list, unless the worker signsThe worker's choice; pay protected 6 months
ArsenicAnnualNone requiredOpinion; no clockNone

A metal level is evidence of exposure, not disease. Only cadmium's triggers oblige anyone to act; the ACGIH BEI is advice.

Chromium (VI)#

Look for nasal ulcers and septal perforation. Portland cement is excluded from the standard; a concrete worker's chromate problem is dermatitis (see Skin disease).

Cadmium#

  • Above urine cadmium 3 µg/g creatinine, blood cadmium 5 µg/L, or β2-microglobulin 300 µg/g creatinine: the employer reassesses exposure, the worker gets a full exam within 90 days, and you decide on removal.
  • Removal is mandatory only when two specimens (the triggering one and the one drawn at that exam) each exceed urine 7, blood 10, or β2-microglobulin 750, and cadmium is over the lower trigger. β2-microglobulin alone never mandates it.
  • Never chelate. The standard forbids it.

Beryllium#

  • Tell the worker they may opt out of any part of the exam.
  • Within 45 days: a full report to the worker and a closed-list opinion to the employer. A limitation, referral, or removal recommendation reaches the employer only with the worker's written authorization.
  • A confirmed positive BeLPT means sensitization, not disease. Chronic beryllium disease is diagnosed at a specialty center.

Recognition only#

No surveillance standard covers these:

  • Manganese: a welder with parkinsonism, tremor, or mood change. Levels exclude nothing. Remove from the fume and refer to neurology.
  • Metal fume fever (zinc) is self-limited. The same picture after brazing or cutting an unknown alloy or cadmium is cadmium fume pneumonitis until proven otherwise (see Chemical exposures).

Pregnancy: ask. Recommend with the basis; the decision is hers.

Kansas: arsenic and mercury aren't reportable to KDHE. Chronic metal disease runs on comp's occupational-disease track, with its one-year limit.

HAZWOPER

Updated 2026-10-28

Who is owed surveillance#

Hazardous waste operations and emergency response: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120 (construction 1926.65). It covers cleanup-site workers, hazardous waste treatment-facility employees, and hazmat response teams. Within those, surveillance is owed to:

  • workers exposed at or above the PEL 30 or more days a year, counted as if no respirator were worn
  • workers wearing a respirator 30 or more days a year
  • anyone injured or symptomatic from possible overexposure in an emergency response or waste operation
  • hazmat team members, by membership alone. No exposure count is needed.

On a fire department, the hazmat team and certified hazmat specialists are the surveillance population. The operations-level engine company is owed its respirator evaluation and, after symptoms, the post-incident consultation, not the periodic exam. The roster is the employer's.

Public employers are covered

Kansas has no OSHA state plan, but an EPA rule (40 CFR 311) applies HAZWOPER to state and local government, and volunteers count as employees. A city, county, or fire district hazmat team, paid or volunteer, is owed this surveillance. It's the one OSHA surveillance program that reaches public employees in Kansas.

When#

ExamWhen
BaselineBefore assignment
PeriodicAt least every 12 months; up to every 2 years only if the examining physician decides a longer interval is appropriate
Leaving coverage (termination or reassignment)Unless examined within 6 months
After symptoms, injury, or emergency overexposureAs soon as possible

The exam#

  • The standard mandates only the history, stressing symptoms from hazardous substances and fitness to wear protective equipment in temperature extremes. Everything else is your call.
  • Tests follow the site's exposure list, not a panel. Where a substance-specific standard reaches the same worker (lead, asbestos), its exam governs its own elements.
  • Fitness for the ensemble is the core question: heavy work in an impermeable suit with SCBA, in the heat. Ask about exertional dyspnea, chest pain, heat intolerance, prior heat illness, and claustrophobia. A limitation is usually a cap on the level of protection (A through D).
  • The respirator questionnaire isn't the HAZWOPER exam, and vice versa. A respirator wearer on a hazmat team needs both, usually at one visit (see Respirator clearance).
  • The employer must send a packet: duties, exposures, protective equipment, prior exams, respirator information. A job title alone doesn't meet the rule.

The written opinion#

Increased risk from the work or respirator use, recommended limitations, and a statement that the worker was informed. Exam results go to the employer only if the worker asks. Unrelated findings never do. There's no medical removal provision.

After an incident, any symptomatic emergency responder, team member or not, is seen as soon as possible (see Chemical exposures). Write it up; it's a surveillance record.

Public Safety

Fire and law enforcement

Updated 2026-10-28

The standards#

These notes cover the standards only. Each department's own protocol sets the battery of tests, and those protocols aren't on this page.

FireLaw enforcement
StandardNFPA 1580 (2025), which replaced NFPA 1582. One set of medical criteria for candidates and incumbents alike.Kansas law, K.S.A. 74-5605(b)(7): the applicant must be free of any physical or mental condition that adversely affects the essential functions. Purely functional; it mandates no tests or thresholds.
Is it law?No. A consensus standard that binds a department only when the department adopts it. No Kansas statute requires it.Yes, for certification by KSCPOST. There's no federal or national standard, and NFPA has no authority over police.
Department protocolsWhere a department's protocol sets the battery, the protocol governsWhere the agency has no protocol, ACOEM's law enforcement guidance is the reference. It's advisory.
Who decidesThe department makes employment decisionsKSCPOST decides certification; the agency decides employment

Kansas: OSHA's respirator, hearing, bloodborne pathogen, and records standards don't bind city or county fire and police agencies. Apply them as best practice, not law. The exception is a fire department's hazmat team, reached by HAZWOPER through EPA's rule.

Fire#

  • Visits: post-offer (only after a documented conditional offer), annual (12 months, plus or minus 3), return to duty, and fitness for duty. The department refers for fitness for duty but doesn't decide it.
  • Outcomes: no restriction, temporary restriction, or permanent restriction, each naming the affected essential job tasks by NFPA 1580 number. Only the physician lifts one. No listed condition is an automatic exclusion. Write "deferred" while the evaluation is incomplete, never "pending clearance."
  • The department gets status and functional impact, never lab values. A diagnosis goes only with the member's written authorization. Behavioral health results never go in identifiable form.
  • A department checkbox form isn't a written medical opinion. Append yours. Claim NFPA 1580 only if every required element was performed and met; otherwise name the ones not performed.
  • A fitness test is never a stress test. A treadmill fitness protocol is scored as fitness, never reported as a cardiac result or as "normal."
  • Cardiac risk: from age 40, calculate 10-year ASCVD risk every year. At 10% to under 20%, NFPA 1580 requires a symptom-limited stress test (with imaging, through Cardiology); at 20% or more, refer to a cardiologist.
  • NFPA 1580 bars a drug test at the annual evaluation.
  • No family history (GINA). If a member volunteers it, don't record it.
  • A positive suicide-risk screen needs a response during the visit, but no positive screen restricts on its own.
  • Pregnancy: she decides. Don't restrict her from a task she's able and willing to do on fetal risk alone.
  • NFPA clearance is not DOT certification. Ask whether the member needs a CDL; see DOT certification.

Law enforcement#

  • Mainly the post-offer candidate exam, plus return to duty and fitness for duty on agency request. No exam before a conditional offer.
  • Outcomes: Medically Qualified; Medically Qualified with Restriction; Medical Evaluation Deferred; Not Medically Qualified. No provisional clearances. A denial rests on your documented functional reasoning alone.
  • The agency gets the determination and functional impact. A diagnosis goes only with the officer's written authorization.
  • The psychological assessment (K.S.A. 74-5605(b)(6)) is a separate assessment, not the physician's job, and nothing in your exam satisfies it. If it's missing, flag it to the agency, citing (b)(6). Don't import the fire behavioral health battery by default.
  • Aerobic testing: the agency's protocol decides who is tested. If it's silent, the examining physician or the clinic protocol decides, and the opinion says which. Whatever test the agency picks is a fitness test, never a stress test, and no standard sets a police MET threshold.
  • Blood pressure: defer at 180/110 or higher. Every stage is referred for treatment.
  • Correctional officer candidates get baseline TB, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C testing. These results may not be used in the hiring decision.
  • Field opioid exposure: incidental skin contact isn't an overdose risk. Naloxone only for objective hypoventilation.
  • Vision has its own standard; see Vision screening.

Practice choice: police aerobic testing

When the agency's protocol is silent: aerobic testing at age 35 or older with a cardiac risk factor, or at 40 or older.

Either one#

  • Acute suicidality in any encounter needs an immediate clinical response.
  • Kansas comp: a firefighter's or officer's heart or stroke claim carries no presumption. It needs a specific work event, the injury within 24 hours of it, and the event as the prevailing factor. Record the event and the time to symptom onset. The KP&F retirement presumption is a pension rule, not comp; give no opinion on it.

Work Capacity

Return to work and fitness for duty

Updated 2026-10-28

Two evaluations, separate from comp care#

Return to work (RTW)Fitness for duty (FFD)
WhoA worker who already has their treating physician's clearanceA current employee whose employer has a documented, objective concern about safe performance
The questionCan they do the actual job at full duty? The employer wants independent confirmation.Can they safely do the job, given the specific concern?

Outcomes for both: fit for full duty; fit with a restriction or accommodation; or not fit, with a reassessment timeline if the condition is expected to change. The employer makes the employment decision.

Is the referral valid?#

A valid FFD referral rests on specific observable facts: dated behavior changes, a safety event, falls.

Not a valid FFD referral

  • "Attitude," production numbers, or coworker complaints with no functional concern. Call the employer before scheduling; with no specific facts raising a medical concern, redirect to HR and document the call.
  • Suspected intoxication. That goes to reasonable-suspicion testing (see Drug and alcohol testing).

FMLA

Passing your evaluation can't be the condition for restoring a worker from FMLA leave; the fitness certification comes from the worker's own provider. State law, a union contract, or the ADA can change that, and the employer and its counsel decide. Ask at intake whether the worker is returning from FMLA. Usually: restore first, then evaluate if there's an objective basis. See Employment laws.

Doing it#

  • No job description, no final clearance. Use Department of Labor physical demand levels as a stand-in and mark the determination pending.
  • Treating clearances: don't rubber-stamp one your exam contradicts. Write a deficit as added job-specific information, not a contradiction. Notify the treating physician of findings beyond their restrictions. A clean exam doesn't override permanent restrictions at MMI without a documented clinical basis.
  • Explore and document accommodation before writing "not fit." Reluctance to return isn't grounds for a restriction.
  • Psychiatric or behavioral concerns are referred out, with a preliminary work status while pending.
  • An FCE is yours to order and interpret. A good FCE doesn't mean the worker is safe from reinjury. "Inconsistent effort" isn't a malingering finding, and the FCE's recommended work level isn't your work status.
  • Pregnancy: under the PWFA, state a limitation even when it temporarily takes an essential function off the job. Never restrict her over her objection on fetal risk alone (see The pregnant worker).

The report#

Everything goes in writing. The report is released only with the worker's signed HIPAA authorization, scoped to functional findings. Write it as if the worker will read it: no opinion on performance, discipline, or credibility, and no verbal side conversations with the employer.

Kansas#

The comp act creates no duty to reinstate; that's a KAAD accommodation question (4 or more employees) and one of employment law. But if a worker refuses accommodated work within the authorized treating physician's restrictions at 90% or more of the pre-injury average weekly wage, the law presumes no wage loss for permanent partial disability (rebuttable). Your recorded restrictions are the measure.

Workers' Compensation

Injury to MMI

Updated 2026-10-29

A workers' comp case, start to finish#

  1. InjuryThe worker gives notice to the employer, within the deadlines in Kansas numbers.
  2. Care directedThe employer or carrier sends the worker to the authorized treating provider.
  3. First visitMechanism in the worker's words, timing, findings, prior history, and work status.
  4. TreatmentConservative first. Restrictions revised every visit. Referrals need authorization.
  5. MMIThe condition has plateaued: as good as treatment will make it. A medical judgment.

This practice stops at MMI. Impairment ratings, settlement, and disputes are handled by others: rating physicians, adjusters, attorneys, and the Kansas Division of Workers Compensation.

Medical causation is the provider's. Legal causation isn't.#

Whether the findings fit the mechanism described is a medical question, and the provider examined the patient, so the provider answers it.

Whether work was the primary cause among all causes is a legal test applied later by others. Kansas calls it the prevailing factor for accidents and repetitive trauma; occupational disease runs on a separate statutory track. The provider doesn't write that conclusion. The provider writes the facts it will be decided on, and they can only be captured on day one:

  • Mechanism
  • Timing
  • Findings, including negatives
  • Prior injuries to the same body part
  • Competing non-work factors

Hold causation open unless the non-work cause is obvious. The common error is closing it early on incomplete facts ("this is arthritis, not the injury"); a degenerative background and a work aggravation often coexist. Where the cause is mixed, write that it's under review pending the records, imaging, or specialist input.

The note is your deposition. Asked in the statute's words whether work was the prevailing factor, answer the medical question (mechanism, findings, consistency, structural change) and say that applying the standard is the adjudicator's.

Impairment and disability#

Impairment is loss of body function. Disability is the gap between that function and what a job requires. A carpenter and an accountant with the same wrist fracture have the same impairment and very different disability.

Function first

Updated 2026-10-29

Two models of the visit#

Most medicine starts with the symptom and aims to relieve it. Occupational medicine starts with function and aims to protect it. ACOEM calls this the function-oriented model, and it changes every part of the visit.

Medical modelFunction-oriented model
HistoryWhat hurts, where, for how longWhat happened, how, and what it has done to the worker's function, including the mechanism and workplace hazards
SocialHabits, family, smokingJob satisfaction, conflict at work, coping. These predict recovery.
ExamHead to toeThe injured part compared with the other side, the areas next to it, and functional tests
RiskHow dangerous the condition and treatment areThat, plus the risk of long-term work disability
DataRecords, tests, consultsThat, plus the job description and worksite information
PlanRelieve the symptomsTreat the condition, return the worker to work, and head off disability

Take the work history#

On any visit where a complaint could have a work cause, ask what the person does. It's the question new providers most often skip.

  • Tasks, one by one, and what's handled nearby. A job title doesn't name an exposure.
  • Pattern: do symptoms ease on weekends and vacations? The pattern raises the question; testing answers it.
  • Other workers from the same space or crew with the same complaint. A second case changes the evaluation.
  • Earlier jobs, protection, and life outside work: an old exposure can cause disease now. Ask what protection was issued and what was actually worn, and about hobbies, home, and second jobs.

Flags for long-term disability#

Chronic work disability is a severe outcome in its own right; ACOEM weighs it with loss of life or limb. Watch for the flags that predict it, and document each one with the plan for it:

Flags for long-term disability

  • Recovery slower than expected for the injury
  • Opioids still in use after 30 days
  • Already off work for weeks
  • No modified duty available
  • Conflict at work

Two or more flags together mark a worker at high risk.

Work status and restrictions

Updated 2026-10-28

Every injury visit ends with a work status#

Full duty, modified duty with restrictions, or off work. "Off work" is a prescription with side effects. The longer someone stays home, the harder coming back gets, so days off are dosed like any other treatment.

  • Default to the least restriction that is safe.
  • Ask what modified duty this employer actually has.
  • Make restrictions specific, functional, and time-limited. Each one is dated, start and end, with the end at the next follow-up, and the worker hears that it ends on that date.
  • The first visit overstates most injuries. Start conservative, recheck, and escalate when the injury needs it. Over-treatment is harm.
  • An ED note saying "off work one week," or a specialist's vague restriction, is information to weigh against this job's demands, not a decision that binds. The treating provider owns work status. Kansas: the authorized treating provider's work-status opinion is presumed determinative (K.S.A. 44-510c(b)(2)(A)).

How to enter and send the work status in Net Health is in Work comp visits.

Risk, capacity, tolerance#

Every restriction rests on one of three things:

MeaningBasis for a restriction?
RiskThe probability of objective harm. The physician's domain.Yes
CapacityMeasured abilityYes
ToleranceThe worker's willingness to work through symptoms. You can't prescribe it.Not by itself

Spot the slow case at the first visit#

Fear of moving, friction at work, no modified duty, and days already lost predict slow recovery. Act on them on day one: the employer call, a real modified-duty job, and an expected return date the worker hears from you. A case running well past its expected duration is a clinical finding, not a scheduling problem.

A regulatory removal isn't a disability#

Some standards remove a worker from a specific exposure on a test result, with no impairment; lead medical removal is the clearest case. Name its regulatory basis and its scope (this exposure, not all work), and say it says nothing about capacity. Earnings are protected only where a standard writes it in. A respirator denial or a post-exposure restriction carries none.

Write restrictions an employer can staff to#

VagueSpecific
Light dutyNo lifting over 20 lb; no ladders
No use of right handRight hand: no forceful gripping; no repetitive gripping; may type and write
Limited standingSit or stand as needed; no standing longer than 30 minutes at a time
Off until seen by orthoRestrictions as above; recheck in 7 days or after the orthopedic visit

Coding comp visits

Updated 2026-11-02

The provider codes the visit#

The provider chooses the billing code for their own visits in Net Health (see Work comp visits).

Practice choice: code on MDM

Comp visits are coded on medical decision making, using the key components of the 2018 CPT E&M guidelines.

The Kansas Schedule of Medical Fees (2024, adopted by K.A.R. 51-9-7) uses CPT 2018, and its E&M ground rules point to the 2018 CPT guidelines for selecting a level. The current (2021) office-visit rules don't apply to a Kansas comp bill.

How the level is set (2018 CPT)#

  • The key components are history, exam, and MDM. A new patient visit needs all three at the level billed; an established patient visit needs two of the three.
