  • MDM rests on the number of diagnoses or management options, the amount and complexity of data reviewed, and the risk of complications, morbidity, or mortality. The MDM level (straightforward, low, moderate, high) needs two of those three.
  • In a comp visit, data includes outside records reviewed and history obtained from someone other than the worker, such as the employer. Record what was reviewed and with whom you spoke.

What a comp note carries#

The note that supports the code is the same note that does the clinical job.

ElementWhat to record
MechanismHow it happened and how work factors relate to the condition. Medical facts, not a legal conclusion.
FunctionWhat the worker can and can't do, what that means for the job, and how it changes from visit to visit
Disability riskThe flags found, and the plan for each (see Function first)
Work planThe return-to-work plan, and who the provider spoke with: employer, adjuster, case manager

Injury codes: the 7th character#

ICD-10 injury codes end in a 7th character that follows the treatment, not the visit count or the provider (ICD-10-CM Guidelines I.C.19.a; fractures, I.C.19.c.1).

  • A: every encounter while the worker is receiving active treatment, whatever the visit number.
  • D: encounters after active treatment is complete, while the injury heals on routine care. Aftercare of an injury takes the injury code with D, not an aftercare Z code.
  • S: a sequela.

The guidelines don't say where active treatment ends, so the note carries the decision. A plan changed at the visit (restrictions adjusted, treatment changed, imaging or a referral ordered) supports A. A plan carried forward unchanged while the injury heals supports D. Switching to D at every follow-up is wrong.

For exam, screening, and exposure codes, see Diagnosis codes.

General and triage

Updated 2026-10-28

The rules for every injury visit#

This covers acute injuries, cumulative or repetitive injuries, and aggravations of pre-existing conditions. The background is in Injury to MMI and Work status and restrictions; the Net Health steps are in Work comp visits.

The core boundary: this practice treats the injury and documents the facts. It doesn't rate impairment or decide compensability. Out of scope: IMEs and ratings, surgery and pre-op "surgical clearance" (redirect to the PCP or the facility's pre-anesthesia clinic), formal RTW and FFD evaluations (see Return to work and fitness for duty), and occupational illness (the exposure lines).

Authorization#

  • Once the employer or carrier directs the worker here, the clinic is the authorized treating provider (ATP) for the whole course of treatment, not one visit. Kansas has no per-visit authorization, so follow-ups need no new one.
  • Authorization comes up again when it was limited (an initial evaluation, or a set number of visits), when a new body part or event appears, when the worker returns after release or MMI, or when you order something that waits on approval (MRI, CT, PT, a specialist). Plain films don't need prior authorization. See Orders and referrals.
  • Authorization doesn't gate the evaluation. Everyone who presents is evaluated, and urgent problems are escalated regardless of paperwork. That's the opposite of a pre-placement exam, where examining before an offer is the violation.

Run the escalation screen on every injury

The typical miss is a presentation that looks falsely reassuring: the pinhole high-pressure injection, the head strike that "seems fine," the eye rinsed at the work site. When in doubt, escalate. Each region's emergencies are in its own note.

What the provider decides#

  • The diagnosis of record. The referral's body part describes; your evaluation defines. Correct the label to match.
  • Medical causation only. Record whether the presentation fits the reported mechanism. Where a prior condition exists, record which applies: a new structural change, a lasting worsening, or a temporary flare that returns to baseline. Reserve "aggravation" for a lasting change.
  • Work status. The ATP's work status opinion is presumed to be determinative under Kansas law, so make it carefully: least restrictive safe duty, quantified, dated to expire at the next follow-up (see Work status and restrictions).
  • MMI, set on the recovery curve, not the calendar. Kansas presumes the employer's treatment obligation ends at MMI. The presumption is easier to overcome when the worker has had, or an ATP has recommended, an invasive or surgical procedure, so document either, and the basis for any expected future care.
  • Not the provider's: recordability (the employer), wage-benefit categories (the adjuster), legal causation, and the intoxication defense.

How Kansas decides a claim#

  • Prevailing factor. Legal causation is the adjudicator's prevailing-factor test, decided on your record. An injury isn't compensable solely because it aggravates a prior condition or makes it symptomatic.
  • Your note can set the date of injury. Cumulative or repetitive trauma runs on the injury track, not the occupational-disease track. Its date of injury is the earliest date a physician takes the worker off work, restricts duty, or tells them it's work-related (or the last day worked, if they've left).
  • ODG measures presumed medical necessity. Care beyond it isn't barred, but the note has to make the case.

Practice choice: MDGuidelines (ACOEM) is the treatment reference

The clinic uses MDGuidelines, which carries the ACOEM guidelines, and has no ODG subscription. Kansas names ODG as its benchmark, so a carrier may cite ODG.

Rules and pitfalls#

  • Report a body-part mismatch the same day, before the first bill. Tell the party directing care. If the referral names the wrong side, examine and document that side too. A new body part is a claim-scope question.
  • Document the mechanism specifically: task, force, position, load in pounds, onset, witnesses, and what the worker has done since. "Injured back at work" isn't a mechanism.
  • No significant functional progress at 4–6 weeks: escalate, and re-examine the diagnosis.
  • A sedating medication in a safety-sensitive worker is a work status decision, made at the same visit. Kansas has no workers' comp drug formulary, and K-TRACS obligations apply.
  • Tell the patient their restrictions before you tell the employer, and never promise outcomes (coverage, surgical results, a full-duty date).

Kansas numbers#

RuleWhat it says
Worker's notice to the employer (K.S.A. 44-520)Due by the earlier of: 30 days from the accident or the date of injury by repetitive trauma; or 20 days after the last day of employment, if no longer employed. Seeking medical treatment doesn't start a deadline; SB 430 (2024) removed that branch. Notice may be oral or written, and goes to the person or department the employer has designated in writing, or a supervisor or manager if no one is designated; telling a coworker isn't notice. Record the date the injury was reported.
Unauthorized medical allowanceA worker may see a provider of their choosing up to $800 (accidents on or after July 1, 2024). It doesn't replace the employer's duty to provide care.
Post-accident drug testSupports the intoxication defense only if collected under six statutory conditions. See Drug and alcohol testing.

Upper extremity

Updated 2026-10-28

Why it's the hardest region#

Shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand. Two reasons: whether the overuse diagnoses (rotator cuff disease, epicondylitis, carpal tunnel, de Quervain's) are work-related is genuinely contested, and several surgical emergencies look trivial at first.

Same-day emergencies

  • High-pressure injection (grease gun, paint sprayer, hydraulic line). A pinhole wound with little pain needs surgical debridement within hours. Don't inject local anesthetic into the digit. Splint, elevate, and transfer now.
  • Fight bite. A laceration over the knuckle is a human bite until proven otherwise. No simple closure.
  • Compartment syndrome, flexor tenosynovitis, septic joint. Transfer. A sheath or palm infection isn't incised or drained before the surgeon sees it, and a septic joint gets no antibiotics before the aspirate.
  • Amputation. Bring the part: wrapped in saline-moistened gauze, sealed in a bag, on ice but never touching it. A part still attached stays attached. Keep the worker NPO.
  • Posterior shoulder dislocation after a seizure or electrical injury. The arm won't externally rotate, and the AP film can look normal. Transfer on suspicion.

Refer within the window#

  • Acute full-thickness rotator cuff tear in a surgical candidate (early MRI). Waiting is itself the harm.
  • Distal biceps rupture
  • Jersey finger (a tendon retracted into the palm is repaired within 7 days) and mallet finger
  • Any motor finding in carpal or cubital tunnel

Suspected scaphoid fracture: thumb-spica splint even with a normal film, and re-image in 1 to 2 weeks. Never discharge on a normal first film.

Don't image into a diagnosis#

  • MRI isn't first-line for gradual shoulder pain: in adults aged 41–76, 96% of shoulders without symptoms had cuff abnormalities on MRI.
  • Nerve conduction studies aren't needed to start treating typical carpal tunnel.
  • Screen the neck. C6 or C7 radiculopathy mimics carpal tunnel, and the two can coexist.

Work status#

One-handed or modified duty beats time off. State it functionally: "no gripping or lifting with the right hand." Relative rest for the shoulder, no routine sling. Epicondylitis runs months, not weeks; say so to the worker and the employer at the first visit.

Causation documentation#

The exposure history tells the cases apart; the diagnosis doesn't.

  • For carpal tunnel the exposure is force, not repetition as such, and keyboard work isn't the exposure.
  • For the shoulder, record arm elevation and load, not "repetitive overhead work."
  • Document competing factors (diabetes, obesity, thyroid disease, pregnancy) with equal care. That's recording the medicine, not taking the employer's side.
  • Kansas: for repetitive trauma, your note can set the date of injury (see How Kansas decides a claim).

Hand-arm vibration syndrome (numb or white fingers in someone who uses vibrating tools) is missed because the early case arrives as finger numbness labeled "carpal tunnel." The restriction names the vibrating tools. Stopping the exposure limits further damage but isn't a cure; tell the worker.

Recordability#

Any splint, cast, or rigid-stay device you recommend is recordable, however briefly it's worn. An elastic wrap, a sleeve, or buddy taping is first aid, as is immobilization used only for transport. See Recordable, reportable, compensable.

Spine

Updated 2026-10-28

The highest-volume complaint#

A back strain after lifting, bending, or twisting (or with no clear event) is the most common presentation in workers' comp. Most workers recover with activity, reassurance, and time: roughly 1 to 6 weeks for a low back or neck strain. Say that expectation out loud, because expectation shapes the course. Don't over-promise after whiplash: about half still report neck pain a year later.

Two messages run together: imaging restraint and the red flag screen.

  • No imaging for typical low back pain without red flags. Early scans find age-related changes common in people without pain, and finding them worsens recovery.
  • Run the red flag screen at every spine visit, not just the first.

Spinal emergencies

  • Cauda equina: new urinary retention (the most consistent feature), saddle numbness, symptoms in both legs, reduced sphincter tone. The window is hours: emergent MRI and transfer to spine. Never hold the transfer for a bladder scan.
  • Unstable fracture, or any spine injury with a neurologic deficit: immobilize and transfer. Image a fall, crush, or axial load with midline tenderness, with a low threshold in older or osteoporotic workers.
  • Infection or cancer: back pain with fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression, a cancer history, weight loss, age over 50, or night or rest pain needs an urgent MRI and referral.
  • Progressive neurologic deficit: escalate, whatever the cause.

Neck, thoracic, and sacrum#

  • Apply the Canadian C-Spine Rule before clearing a traumatic neck.
  • Screen every neck for myelopathy, recording each sign as present, absent, or unable to assess. Any upper motor neuron sign means a cervical MRI. Suspected myelopathy means no safety-sensitive work, heights, or driving until it's evaluated.
  • Thoracic pain that is non-mechanical (constant, at rest, waking the worker) is a red flag until proven otherwise. "Muscle pain between the shoulder blades" can be cardiac, aortic, pulmonary, or GI.
  • Sacral insufficiency or stress fracture: suspect it when a posterior pelvic "strain" doesn't progress. Plain films are often negative; MRI makes the diagnosis.

Care and work status#

  • Stay active; bed rest is harmful.
  • An NSAID is first-line; acetaminophen where an NSAID doesn't suit.
  • Muscle relaxants are second-line and short-term. ACOEM advises against taking one before a shift, driving, or safety-sensitive work, so set that restriction at the same visit.
  • Add PT for workers not improving on schedule, not on day one.
  • Opioids aren't first-line and are largely avoided.
  • Restrict the loads that provoke symptoms while keeping the worker at work. Stenosis limits standing and walking; coccyx pain limits sitting (a cushion and permission to stand are often enough); a sacral fracture limits weight-bearing.

Documentation and recordability#

  • Waddell signs are recorded as a count and category: an observation, never a verdict on honesty or effort.
  • On a degenerative background, record the causation category (see What the provider decides).
  • Prescription medication, formal PT, or an injection is beyond first aid. A restriction on a routine job function beyond the day of injury makes the case recordable on its own. A strain managed with OTC medication at label strength may stay first aid. See Recordable, reportable, compensable.

Lower extremity

Updated 2026-10-28

The biggest mechanical caseload#

Hip, knee, ankle, and foot: mostly sprains, strains, tendinopathies, contusions, and stable fractures. The ankle sprain is the highest-volume injury in this region, and plantar fasciitis is the top foot complaint in a standing workforce.

The Ottawa knee and ankle rules decide whether an x-ray is needed. Don't MRI knees reflexively: degenerative meniscal tears are common in workers over 50 who have no symptoms.

Limb-threatening: recognize and transfer

  • Knee dislocation. It often reduces on its own and looks like a bad sprain. Treat any multiligament knee as a reduced dislocation and work it up for vascular injury (pulses, ankle-brachial index). Normal pulses don't exclude arterial injury.
  • Compartment syndrome. Pain out of proportion, and pain on passive stretch. Pulselessness comes late.
  • Pelvic ring fracture, open fracture, limb ischemia
  • Septic joint. No antibiotics before the aspirate; the clinic doesn't aspirate. Splint and transfer.
  • Hip fracture after a fall. Don't stand the worker up. A normal film doesn't settle it if they still can't bear weight.
  • DVT after injury or immobilization: same-day ultrasound, and no return to work until a clot is excluded.

Referrals#

  • Prompt: complete Achilles rupture and complete proximal hamstring avulsion (both time-sensitive), extensor mechanism disruption (urgent), a locked knee.
  • Orthopedics: Lisfranc injury, syndesmotic diastasis, and displaced, unstable, intra-articular, or open fractures. A Jones fracture often needs surgical fixation.

Classic misses and the habits that prevent them#

  • Lumbar root pain treated as hip pain for months. The straight-leg raise doesn't reach L2–L3; run the femoral stretch test.
  • A false-positive ACL finding. Check for posterior sag (a PCL injury) before any Lachman or drawer.
  • A Maisonneuve fracture. Palpate the proximal fibula on every ankle.
  • Lisfranc missed on a non-weight-bearing film. Get weight-bearing views.
  • A Jones fracture called an avulsion. It goes on to nonunion.
  • A stress fracture "ruled out" by an early normal film.

Work status#

  • State weight-bearing status explicitly. "Light duty" without it isn't usable.
  • Instability (ladders, uneven ground) is a separate restriction from weight-bearing.
  • Footwear is often the whole restriction.
  • Set duration expectations at the first visit. A stable high ankle sprain takes roughly five to nine weeks to full function; a lateral sprain about two weeks.
  • Driving: with an Achilles rupture or an ankle or lower-leg fracture, no driving while the right foot is immobilized, or while either foot is immobilized if the vehicle has a clutch.

Recordability#

An elastic wrap or a soft brace without stays is first aid. A cast, a rigid boot, or a brace with rigid stays is recordable once recommended, however briefly it's worn, and so are crutches you recommend or provide. Withholding an indicated device to keep a case off the log is the failure this rule exists to prevent. See Recordable, reportable, compensable.

Kansas#

An injury from idiopathic causes is excluded. Whether a fall was idiopathic (a knee that gives way on level ground) or a fall from or against a work hazard is decided on the record, so record what the worker fell from or against and what came just before the fall.

Head injury and concussion

Updated 2026-10-28

Two jobs#

Recognize the rare intracranial emergency in the first minutes. For everyone else, decide honestly whether there is a concussion, and manage the worker back to work.

Transfer by EMS now

  • GCS below 15 at your first assessment, or any decline. Don't wait for it to clear.
  • A focal deficit: unequal pupils, asymmetric weakness, new aphasia, gaze deviation
  • A seizure, repeated vomiting, or a worsening or severe headache
  • Signs of a skull fracture (raccoon eyes and Battle's sign can take a day to appear), or a penetrating injury
  • "Got better, then got worse"

To the ED today, accompanied and not driving

Even without the signs above: any loss of consciousness or amnesia, a persistent headache, any vomiting, prior brain surgery, a bleeding disorder, intoxication, your own continuing concern, or any anticoagulant, or any antiplatelet other than aspirin alone, after even a minor mechanism.

Is it a concussion?#

  • Three classifications: concussion diagnosed; suspected (managed as concussion, not recorded as confirmed); or criteria not met. A worker who presents late with symptoms only and no documented sign is suspected.
  • Examine at the first contact. Exam findings lose sensitivity over the first 72 hours.
  • Get collateral history early from a supervisor or coworker. A witnessed sign establishes the diagnosis; "seemed fine" excludes nothing.
  • "No head strike" doesn't exclude a mechanism. Acceleration or deceleration without contact qualifies.
  • Over-diagnosis harms. A brief "saw stars" in a worker who was oriented right away, with no amnesia and no persistent symptom, isn't a concussion. Mimics: cervicogenic headache (the most common), BPPV (run a Dix-Hallpike before blaming the brain), migraine, syncope that caused the fall, intoxication.
  • The tools have limits. A negative CT doesn't exclude concussion; don't order an MRI to look for one. Record VOMS values and the change from baseline, never "VOMS positive." No score clears anyone for safety-sensitive work.

Care and work status#

  • A day or two of relative rest, then gradual activity kept below symptom level. No strict rest.
  • Modify, don't remove. Restrict by hazard (driving, heights, machinery, confined space, firearms), not by diagnosis.
  • Never clear to safety-sensitive duty on a resting symptom report alone. The worker must be symptom-free at rest and with exertion, with a normal cognitive screen and vestibular-ocular findings, and you confirm readiness for the specific task.
  • Don't infer a CDL certification date from symptom resolution (see DOT certification). Formal fitness-for-duty clearance is a separate evaluation (see Return to work and fitness for duty).
  • Written return precautions are required, and documented.

The course#

Most resolve within a couple of weeks. ACOEM's outer bound for an uncomplicated mild TBI is one to three months. Early follow-up is every one to five days.

Four weeks is a decision point, not a failure. A worker not improving by then (or worsening at any point) is referred, and the diagnosis is reconsidered. A worker still symptomatic but improving hasn't "failed to recover" and shouldn't be told so. A new neurologic finding at any time goes out emergently.

Recordability and Kansas#

  • Loss of consciousness makes a case recordable by itself, so document whether it truly happened. Concussion itself isn't on OSHA's significant-diagnosis list; the restrictions that follow usually make the case recordable.
  • Kansas: an acute head injury is an accident, on the injury track (see How Kansas decides a claim).

Eye injury

Updated 2026-10-28

The common one#

"Something flew in my eye," from grinding, drilling, or sanding. Ask what the material was and how fast it was moving, every time: the mechanism, not the appearance, flags the dangerous eye.

Visual acuity first, every time, each eye, recorded by the line read. "Vision grossly intact" isn't enough.

Chemical splash: irrigate before you evaluate

  • Irrigate copiously and sweep the fornices for particulate; cement and lime keep burning.
  • Continue until the ocular-surface pH is 7.0–7.2 and holds on a recheck at least 5 minutes after irrigation stops.
  • Alkali is worse than acid. A white, blanched eye after alkali is worse, not better.
  • Hydrofluoric acid is transferred on the product, however the eye looks. It's in rust removers, aluminum brighteners, wheel and masonry cleaners, and glass etch.

Open globe or intraocular foreign body

Suspect it from the mechanism (metal on metal, grinding, hammering, a high-speed projectile), not the appearance; vision may be near normal. If you suspect it:

  • Stop examining: no pressure on the globe, no tonometry.
  • Apply a rigid shield, not a patch. Nothing by mouth. No drops. Update tetanus.
  • Arrange emergent ophthalmology transfer. CT of the orbit with thin cuts is the study; no MRI if metal is possible.

Other emergencies and urgent referrals: retrobulbar hemorrhage (a tense, proptotic eye with falling vision), any sudden significant loss of vision, a thermal burn of the cornea or conjunctiva (cool with irrigation, then transfer), any hyphema, and a blowout fracture with entrapment.

Abrasions#

  • Never send topical anesthetic home. It's toxic to the cornea.
  • Antibiotics: a routine clean abrasion gets ordinary broad coverage, short course. A contact lens abrasion gets pseudomonas coverage (a topical fluoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside): a different drug, not a longer course, and never patched. Cover a contaminated abrasion. After a metallic foreign body from grinding or hammering, cover, recheck the next day, and ask the penetration question again.
  • A small, clean, peripheral abrasion with good acuity that you can recheck the next day may be observed without an antibiotic, because it's low-risk, never to keep a case off the log.
  • Routine patching isn't recommended. If a cycloplegic is used, short-acting only. Ointment blurs, so choose the vehicle against the job.

Other pitfalls#

  • Traumatic iritis comes back one to three days after blunt trauma: worse pain, consensual photophobia, a clean fluorescein. It's referred; ocular steroids aren't started in the clinic.
  • Welder's flash shows up 6 to 12 hours after exposure, in both eyes, and resolves in about 24 to 48 hours.
  • Subconjunctival hemorrhage alone is full duty with no treatment. After high-energy trauma, or with no visible back border, think ruptured globe.

Recordability and Kansas#

  • Removal by irrigation or a cotton swab is first aid. Removal with a needle, burr, forceps, or other instrument is recordable, and so are prescription drops (antibiotic or cycloplegic). A restriction past the day of injury that affects a routine job function, or a day away, records the case whatever the treatment. See Recordable, reportable, compensable.
  • Kansas: vision loss from a work injury is compensable as a scheduled loss.

Wounds and burns

Updated 2026-10-28

What decides these cases#

Not closure technique. What matters is recognizing the small wound that isn't small, matching the disposition to the job rather than the wound size, and getting the OSHA first-aid line right without letting it drive care.

Wounds that are really emergencies

  • High-pressure injection and fight bites (see Upper extremity)
  • Any nerve, tendon, or vascular involvement. Test tendons against resistance before calling a wound simple. Flexor tendon repair has a time window; digital nerve injuries go to hand surgery.
  • Flexor tenosynovitis and deep palmar space infection: hand surgery
  • Suspected necrotizing infection: same-hour transfer

Every wound#

  • Check tetanus status. Prophylactic antibiotics aren't routine for clean lacerations.
  • Retained foreign body is among the most common wound malpractice claims. Explore, image when a radiopaque fragment is plausible, and document "explored, no foreign body identified."
  • A puncture through the sole of a shoe can cause a Pseudomonas bone or joint infection days to weeks later.
  • Fingertips: trephine a subungual hematoma under an intact, adherent nail, whatever its size. Refer a fingertip with exposed bone.
  • Abscess: antibiotics aren't drainage. A fluctuant collection is drained at the visit and cultured; antibiotics are added only for a stated reason. Draining and prescribing are both recordable, so the log is no reason to choose.

The OSHA line#

  • Sutures, staples, and tissue glue are medical treatment (recordable). Steri-Strips and butterfly closures are first aid.
  • An injected local anesthetic is a prescription drug, so cleaning a wound under it makes the case recordable.
  • Never use Steri-Strips on a wound that needs sutures to keep it off the log.
  • For the employer's OSHA reporting, a fingertip amputation counts as an amputation, with or without bone loss.

See Recordable, reportable, compensable.

Burns#

Burns follow the American Burn Association's two-tier referral criteria. Call the burn center early.

  • Immediate consultation, with transfer considered: any full-thickness burn; partial-thickness burns of 10% of body surface or more; deep burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum, or a joint; suspected inhalation; high-voltage electrical injury.
  • Consultation: smaller partial-thickness burns, any burn that may be deep, low-voltage electrical injury.
  • Circumferential burns aren't on the ABA list but are transferred on their own clinical grounds.
  • Chemical burns are routed on the agent (see Chemical exposures).

Practice choice: the burn center

Burn transfers go to the Burnett Burn Center at The University of Kansas Health System.

Electrical injury#

The ED, whatever the skin looks like, for high voltage, loss of consciousness, an arrhythmia or chest pain, tetany with prolonged contact, a fall or blast, dark urine, a neurologic deficit, pregnancy, or lightning. Low-voltage contact stays in clinic only if the worker has no symptoms, a normal exam, and a normal ECG.

Kansas#

A wet-work skin condition with no injury behind it is an occupational disease, not an injury (see Skin disease).

Chest and abdomen

Updated 2026-10-28

What decides these cases#

Trunk-wall injuries and groin hernias. Several emergencies look fine at the first exam: a delayed pneumothorax or hemothorax after rib fractures, a delayed splenic rupture after a flank fall. Re-screen at every return. Give written return precautions, and follow up within days on blunt trunk trauma that wasn't imaged.

EMS now

  • Respiratory distress, low saturation, asymmetric breath sounds, subcutaneous emphysema, a flail segment
  • Guarding, rigidity, or rebound; a tender abdomen under a seat-belt, strap, or handlebar mark; unstable vital signs; left-shoulder-tip pain after a left-sided impact
  • Any abdominal pain after blunt trauma in a worker on anticoagulants
  • An irreducible hernia that is tense, tender, or discolored, or with vomiting or obstipation
  • Any wound that may have entered the chest or abdomen (stab, impalement, nail gun): trauma center
  • A sternal fracture (step-off or crepitus): ED for an ECG and cardiac evaluation, however well the worker looks

Chest pain called a "pulled muscle"#

Reproducible chest-wall tenderness lowers the chance of a cardiac cause; it doesn't exclude one. Exertional onset, radiation, sweating, dyspnea, nausea, or pressure-type pain goes to the ED by EMS. The clinic can't rule out a coronary syndrome, normal ECG or not.

Rib fractures#

  • The diagnosis is clinical. The chest film is for pneumothorax and hemothorax.
  • Never strap the chest.
  • ED for the admission decision: age 65 or older, three or more fractured ribs, chronic lung disease, anticoagulation, or low saturation.
  • Restrictions cover lifting, twisting, overhead work, and a tight-fitting respirator while a full breath is limited.
  • A rib fracture is recordable on diagnosis. Don't soften it to "contusion" (see Recordable, reportable, compensable).

Abdominal wall#

Fever, vomiting, bowel or urinary change, or migrating pain isn't a strain. A rectus sheath hematoma that is enlarging, or in a worker on anticoagulants, is a transfer.

Inguinal hernia: the contested lifting claim#

Most hernias are revealed by a lift, not created by it. Examine both sides, standing and supine, and record:

  • the worker's own words and the timing
  • any bulge or groin symptom before the event, on either side
  • prior repair, reducibility, and mechanism

Write no conclusion that the lift did or didn't cause it.

  • A symptomatic reducible hernia in a worker whose job loads the trunk is referred for repair. Watchful waiting is an accepted option for a man with few or no symptoms.
  • Restrictions follow the symptoms and the job, reviewed each visit. After repair, the surgeon's instructions govern.
  • Kansas: a traumatic hernia is limited to medical care, temporary total disability while the worker can't work, and 12 weeks' compensation if it's inoperable. Unreasonably refusing repair of an operable hernia forfeits all benefits, so record operability, the repair recommendation, and the worker's response.

Injury visits at this clinic

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

What this clinic does in a workers' comp injury visit. How a case runs is in Injury to MMI; how the visit runs in Net Health is in Work comp visits. Authorizations are in Authorizations, and cases that belong elsewhere are in Cases we don't handle.

Seen as soon as possible#

Injuries are seen as soon as possible. Care doesn't wait for authorization; see Care doesn't wait for authorization.

The employer's protocol#

Each employer's protocol is in Net Health. For injuries it says who to contact, what accommodations the employer offers, and the employer's post-injury drug and alcohol testing preferences. Check it at every injury visit.

Restrictions end at the follow-up date#

Practice choice: restrictions end at follow-up

Work restrictions end on the follow-up date. The patient is told at the visit that the restrictions have an end date, and the Work Status Expiration instruction block says they end if the patient doesn't come back (see Instruction blocks). An end date keeps restrictions from running on when return visits are delayed again and again.

Cases we don't handle

Updated 2026-10-22

When this applies#

A patient whose case belongs somewhere else. The aim is to recognize it at the desk or in the first minutes of the visit.

Federal workers' comp (Department of Labor)#

Federal civilian employees are not covered by Kansas workers' comp. Their injuries fall under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act (FECA), run by the Department of Labor's Office of Workers' Compensation Programs (OWCP). The clinic doesn't handle these cases.

  • Who: employees of a federal agency, such as the Postal Service, the VA, TSA, or the FAA.
  • What it looks like at the desk: a federal employer, or a form numbered CA-. CA-1 is a traumatic injury claim, CA-2 an occupational disease claim, CA-16 an authorization for a visit, and CA-17 a duty status report.
  • Why it isn't ours: FECA has its own rules, its own forms, and its own provider enrollment.

The Department of Labor runs other programs too: longshore and harbor workers, energy employees, and black lung. None of them is Kansas workers' comp.

Other work the clinic doesn't do#

  • Independent medical exams (IMEs) and impairment ratings
  • Surgical clearance. Redirect it to the patient's own clinician or the facility's pre-anesthesia clinic.

Our clinics

Updated 2026-11-01

Three clinics#

Providers work at three occupational health clinics: the Medical Pavilion, KU MedWest, and Olathe.

The Pavilion is not the Olathe clinic

The Medical Pavilion is on Olathe Boulevard in Kansas City, KS. The Olathe clinic is in the city of Olathe.

  • The Pavilion and MedWest take walk-in and scheduled visits. Olathe takes walk-ins.
  • Drug testing: at the Pavilion, patients arrive by 6 pm. At MedWest, they arrive at least an hour before closing. Olathe accepts drug screens until 6 pm.
  • Parking is free at all occupational health locations.
  • Email: OCC@KUMC.edu.
  • Sodexo and Vanguard contractors are typically seen at MedWest. See Health system contractors.

The health system has one more occupational health location, St. Rose Medical Pavilion in Great Bend. It isn't one of these three clinics.

Front Office

ID and registration

Updated 2026-10-22

When this applies#

What the front desk checks at registration, and what the provider needs to know about it. At check-in the front desk uploads the authorization and the ID into Net Health (see Employment exams, Work comp visits, DOT exams).

ID by visit#

VisitID
DOT examThe driver's license. The front desk enters the number, the state, and whether it's a CDL. The provider checks the license in Images.
DOT drug or alcohol testThe federal rule: see Rules
Any other visit or collectionThe practice choice below

Practice choice: ID for non-DOT visits

For a non-DOT collection or visit, the clinic accepts a photo ID or the employer's confirmation of identity.

DOT drivers#

  • No driver's license number: enter NONE, and enter the state the driver will be moving to.

Offer status#

For a post-offer exam, the offer is confirmed at registration. If it isn't, the applicant goes back to registration before any part of the exam. See Pre-placement exams.

Authorizations

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

Workers' comp injury visits. The employer or carrier sends an authorization. The front desk handles authorizations, including a wrong one. It uploads the authorization at check-in, and the provider checks at the visit that it covers the body part (see Work comp visits).

One authorization covers the treatment#

Kansas has no per-visit authorization. When the employer or carrier directs the worker here, the clinic becomes the authorized treating provider for the whole course of treatment. Return visits for the same injury need no new authorization.

Authorization becomes a question again when:

  • The authorization was limited to an initial evaluation or a set number of visits
  • A new body part or a new event appears
  • The worker returns after release or after MMI
  • The provider orders something that waits on approval: MRI or CT, PT, or a specialist referral (see Orders and referrals)

Plain films are on site and need no prior authorization.

Care doesn't wait for authorization#

Practice choice: patient care comes first

The provider evaluates the patient and documents the encounter as usual while the front desk works on the authorization. The two run in parallel, and care is never delayed waiting for authorization. If the case turns out not to be work related, or the company refuses to authorize, the provider still documents the injury, manages anything urgent, and helps direct care to the right place.

Kansas: an employer that sends a worker to find out whether a complaint is work related pays for that visit, even if it turns out not to be (Kansas Schedule of Medical Fees, introduction). See Who pays.

When the authorization is wrong#

  • Wrong body part or side: examine and document what the worker presents with, including the other side if the referral names the wrong one. Report the mismatch the same day to the party directing care, before the first bill.
  • A new body part is a question of the claim's scope, not just a correction.

Health System

TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

Post-offer exams for TUKHS and UKP. The visit runs as in Employment exams. This note covers what's specific to these clients.

Job descriptions#

  • For TUKHS, Employee Health shares a tracker with the job description links embedded. Use it to check the physical requirements, the vision requirements, and whether a fit test is needed.
  • UKP has no job descriptions.
  • If the patient can't meet the requirements, print the job description for them (see below).

Labs#

The basic labs are titers for measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, and hepatitis B, and a QFT for TB surveillance. When each titer is ordered, and what counts as proof of immunity, is in Health care worker exams.

Fit testing#

A fit test is required for patient-facing positions. When a prior fit test is accepted is in Health care worker exams.

Vision#

  • Whether depth perception passes depends on the job description and its requirements.
  • If the patient fails depth perception, repeat the test with them. They often do much better on the repeat.

Clearance letter#

Send it at the end of the visit, following Work clearance letters. Recipients are in Where results and letters go.

  • Delete any part of the letter template that doesn't apply.
  • Include "TB surveillance pending."
  • During influenza season (November 1 to March 31), clearance follows the KU Flu Policy. Note in the letter whether the patient is vaccinated or has an exemption.

When the patient doesn't meet the job requirements#

This is most often vision.

  1. Print the job description and give it to the patient with the health care provider accommodation form.
  2. In the clearance letter, state that the patient is not cleared. Don't give details of the medical condition of concern.

The Restriction or Limitation History section of the patient's history helps here. A temporary or permanent restriction, or a condition that may require a special work assignment, likely means the patient needs accommodation paperwork. Talk to the patient: they may have answered yes by mistake, or it may not limit them in this job.

QFT results#

QFT and titer results arrive in the Net Health in-basket. When a QFT result arrives, check the letter from the visit to see the client.

  • TUKHS, normal: no result note is needed. Select Done. Employee Health reviews these.
  • UKP, normal: write the result note "Negative QFT. UKP." and route it to clinic staff.
  • Anything else routes as in Where results and letters go.

After the provider routes them, clinic staff handle TUKHS results and refer UKP and GME results to the right place.

Titer results#

  • TUKHS and UKP pay for any needed vaccines. Vaccines are not required for employment, even if titers are low.
  • When reviewing titer results in the in-basket, type a short note for the patient: which immunities they have, which they lack, and what vaccination is recommended. What to recommend for each low titer is in Low titers.

Drug screens (TUKHS)#

  • TUKHS also does drug screens. These are separate visits, sometimes before the exam but usually with it.
  • Providers do not order drug screens or EBTs.
  • Providers don't co-sign drug screens.

Health and Wellness visits

Updated 2026-10-10

When this applies#

Health and Wellness (H&W) visits. They are a catch-all visit type, mostly for TUKHS.

Offsite physicals#

  • New hires who live outside the local area can do their physical offsite. The offsite services are mainly the physical, vision, and QFT.
  • Most still need titers, and a fit test if it applies.
  • Employee Health receives all offsite physical information and uploads it to a Teams group that occupational health providers can open.
Finding offsite results
  1. In Teams, open the EH/TA Onboarding Communication UKHS team and select the Out of State Candidate Info channel. It looks locked, but providers have access.
  2. Select Files. This lists folders by name.
  3. Open the patient's folder. It holds whatever testing was done offsite. If something isn't there, assume it wasn't done.

Patients sometimes bring vaccine records to the H&W visit.

The visit#

  • Typical rooming, such as vitals and history, is not done. The patient has already had their physical and is cleared.
  • No clearance letter or evaluation is needed. These visits are checked in as provider visits, but they are not provider visits.

Return visits#

  • The same visit type is used when a patient returns, for example to repeat a failed vision test or for labs that couldn't be drawn the first time. The visit notes usually say why they're there.
  • If a vision failure resolves on return, you don't need to see the patient, unless you want to tell them they're cleared. Send an updated work clearance stating they have no restrictions (see Work clearance letters).

Health system contractors

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

Sodexo and Vanguard. They are contractors who work within the health system, and they are typically seen at Medwest.

Services#

  • They must have an authorization to be seen.
  • They get the same services as a TUKHS post-offer, even when the authorization doesn't show it: the physical, QFT, titers, and a fit test if it applies. See TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams.
  • The clinic gives them influenza vaccines.

Job descriptions and fit tests#

  • Sodexo job descriptions come from Sodexo.
  • There are no job descriptions for Vanguard. Ask the Vanguard post-offer what their job will be.
  • Fit tests are for patient-facing jobs. Use your judgment.
  • They all complete the "short" respirator questionnaire for fit testing.

QFT results#

When a QFT result for either contractor reaches the in-basket, sign it and route it to clinic staff with a note saying it's negative and which client it is, so the result can be sent to the client. Anything else routes as in Where results and letters go.

Employee Health

Updated 2026-10-10

When this applies#

Contacting TUKHS Employee Health, and deciding what goes to them.

About Employee Health#

  • Employee Health used to be combined with occupational health. It now falls under HR.
  • The former SW Market (Olathe) Employee Health nurses are now part of TUKHS Employee Health.

Reaching them#

  • Teams, during business hours (8 to 4:30). They respond quickly. Use the OH/EH combined chat, or message them individually.
  • Direct line: 913-942-6630.
  • Email: employeehealth@kumc.edu.

What to ask them#

  • SW Market-specific questions, such as whether a patient has a hepatitis B titer on record from an Olathe post-offer: ask the nurses who came from SW Market Employee Health.
  • For TUKHS employees, whether a referral was approved, or whether there are results from a referral.

What goes to them#

What patients should be sent to Employee Health for is in When to refer to Employee Health.

Exposure questionnaires#

If the medical director is unavailable and there's an exposure in the health system, Employee Health may ask you to review exposure questionnaires.

EPIC

Orders in EPIC

Updated 2026-10-10

When this applies#

When a visit needs an x-ray, a stress test, or an EKG. Radiologists and cardiologists read these, and the rest of the hospital works in EPIC, so the order and the result have to be in EPIC. The order is also recorded in Net Health.

The steps below are written for an x-ray. They're being rewritten to be clearer and to cover stress tests and EKGs.

Who#

The provider and the front desk (PSR).

Steps#

  1. Tell the PSRs you need to place an order in EPIC. They may need to add the patient to EPIC.
  2. While you wait, add the order in Net Health for the record.
  3. Once the patient is in EPIC, create an orders-only encounter and place the order:
    1. Select Chart and enter the MR number.
    2. Select EPIC at the top left.
    3. Search Orders Only.
    4. Select the patient again.
    5. Select KUMW OCH Clinic.
    6. Request break the glass. This is expected: it's the only way the clinic can place orders in EPIC.
    7. Select OC → Dept.
    8. Add the diagnosis at the bottom.
    9. Add the order at the bottom left.
    10. Sign.
  4. Tell the PSRs the order is in EPIC. For an x-ray, post the request in the Teams X-ray chat with the MR number.
  5. For an x-ray, view the images in Work Tools → Health System Links → Image Viewer.
  6. Do not print your read for upload into EPIC.

Net Health (formerly Agility)

  • Employment exams
  • Work comp visits
  • DOT exams
  • Respirator exams
  • Tasks

Employment exams

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

Employment exams in Net Health, other than DOT exams. For DOT, see DOT exams. For the respirator form, see Respirator exams. For what's specific to TUKHS and UKP, see TUKHS and UKP post-offer exams. For what the employer may ask and learn, including why family history is left out, see Employment laws.

Who#

Front desk (PSR), clinical staff, and the provider.

Steps#

Check-in (PSR)
  1. Upload the authorization and ID.
  2. Review the authorization.
  3. Print the applicable forms, such as the fit test form or TB questionnaire.
  4. Print the encounter form with all standard services selected.
Clinical staff
  1. Review the encounter form and request orders from the provider in Teams.
Provider: orders
  1. Check the company protocol in Net Health for this employer's exam.
  2. Select Template at the top.
  3. Select the Visit tab. If the provider name is wrong, select Edit and correct it.
  4. Under the Assessment tab, add the ICD-10 code (see ICD-10 codes).
  5. Under the Orders tab, place the orders. Common orders: hepatitis B, MMR, varicella, influenza, and fit test.
  6. If a TB skin test is ordered, order both the test and the PPD medication.
  7. Tell clinical staff the orders are in.
Clinical staff
  1. Move the patient to the right area on the Whiteboard.
  2. Complete the orders, vitals, vision, and PMH.
  3. Place the chart in the rack.
  4. Change the status to ready for provider.
Provider: exam and documentation
  1. Change the status to with provider on the Whiteboard.
  2. Review the PMH, vitals, and any testing, using the Attest to review of ___ buttons.
  3. See the patient.
  4. Let the patient leave, and change the location to discharged.
  5. Complete the ROS and physical.
  6. Enter the diagnosis or assessment in the large text box under Assessment.
  7. Enter the plan in the large text box under Instructions. This box does not print on the patient's copies.
  8. Select Patient Instructions and enter the patient's instructions there. Instructions left in the large box never reach the patient.
  9. Select Work Status, then Assessment of Work Status, and enter the status. For KU, add QFT Pending.
    • Standard text: "The applicant has no findings which would prohibit them from safely performing the job described."
  10. Send the certification letter: follow Work clearance letters.
Provider: complete the note and charges
  1. Select Build Note, review the note, and sign it.
  2. Mark the note Complete, then select Save and Done.
  3. Confirm the charges. Providers charge every post-offer and DOT exam in Net Health as part of the documentation. For a DOT exam, marking Exam-DOT complete is the charge (see DOT exams). For any other physical: on the Procedures tab, select Edit on the exam charge and change Result from ? to C.

Work comp visits

Updated 2026-11-01

When this applies#

Workers' compensation injury visits in Net Health. For what goes into the work status, see Work status and restrictions; for coding, see Coding comp visits.

Who#

Front desk (PSR), clinical staff, and the provider.

Steps#

Check-in (PSR)
  1. Upload the authorization to see, the authorization to treat, and the ID.
Clinical staff
  1. Move the patient to the right area on the Whiteboard and room them.
  2. Complete the HPI.
  3. Change the status to ready for provider.
  4. Place the chart in the rack.
Provider: visit

  2. Review the authorization to make sure the body part is included (see Authorizations).
  3. Check the company protocol in Net Health for this employer's instructions.
  4. Review the HPI and PMH.
  5. See the patient.
  6. Select Assessment and add the ICD-10 diagnoses. To find a code, search the web for the diagnosis and "ICD-10." The 7th character follows the treatment, not the visit number: keep A while the plan is still changing (see Injury codes: the 7th character).
  7. If x-rays are needed, follow Orders in EPIC.

Provider: complete the note
  1. Complete and review the remaining portions of the note.
  2. Select Build Note.
  3. Code the E&M.
  4. Sign.

Respirator exams

Respirator and asbestos exams in Net Health. What the clearance must decide and say is in Respirator clearance and Asbestos.

The form#

The Respirator Clearance form is in Forms, under PreFill Print. If it wasn't printed at check-in, open it from the Forms tab. It is not an interactive form like the DOT forms.

Tasks

Work clearance letters

Updated 2026-10-10

When this applies#

Post-offer exams, firefighters, police, and return to work. Used from Employment exams.

Who#

The provider.

Steps#

Build the clearance text
  1. Complete the exam.
  2. In the Assessment of Work Relatedness and Work Status tab, select the Work Clearance Template (Smart Form Charting Wizard).
  3. Complete the fields (see the table below). Provider Comments is required.
  4. Select Done. The text populates in the note.
Create and send the letter
  1. Copy the clearance text.
  2. From the open chart, select View Chart.
  3. Select Print a Letter at the bottom of the demographics page.
  4. Select the magnifying glass next to Notice ID.
  5. Select Work Clearance Letter.
  6. Select the Notice tab at the top, and choose:
    • Greeting: formal (Dear Mr/Ms) or informal (Dear John).
    • Destination: home address or Unit / Work Address.
  7. Paste the clearance text into the letter body, between Name: [&Employee Name] and the "For any questions or concerns…" paragraph. The footer already carries the clinic's contact details and the electronic signature.
  8. Type your name at the bottom.
  9. Select Sign.
  10. Select the envelope icon in the top-right toolbar.
  11. Enter the email address, or pick an entity on record from the panel on the right of the email window. Recipients by client are in Where results and letters go. Copy yourself.
  12. Enter the subject line as Last name (Company). The subject is prefixed [Secure].
  13. Select OK at the bottom right. The pop-up now shows EMail instead of Print in the right corner.
  14. Select EMail. When the letter pops up, select the printer symbol at the top. This sends the email.
  15. Return to the chart and build the note.

Don't print before emailing

Don't select Print until the email is set up. Once EMail is selected, the printer symbol sends the letter to the email address.

Orders and referrals

When this applies#

Placing orders and referrals in Net Health, including PT and advanced imaging for work comp. For x-rays, stress tests, and EKGs, see Orders in EPIC.

Wizards#

Quick reference
ICD-10 codes

KU's codes. The exam or screening code is listed first and a finding second. What each code covers, and why, is in Diagnosis codes.

Visit or serviceICD-10
Pre-employment or post-offer examZ02.1
Periodic exam of a current employeeZ02.89
Fire: post-offer examZ02.1
Fire: annual examZ02.89
Police: post-offer examZ02.1
DOTZ02.4
Respirator clearance, fitness for duty, return-to-work clearanceZ02.89
AudiogramZ01.10; Z01.118 with findings
Vision screenZ01.00; Z01.01 with findings
ImmunizationsZ23
Behind on required vaccinesZ28.39, with Z23
Antibody titerZ01.84
TB screen, no exposureZ11.7
TB chest x-ray, prior positiveZ11.1
TB exposure: first and 8–10 week testsZ20.1
Positive TB skin test / positive IGRAR76.11 / R76.12
Bloodborne pathogen exposureZ77.21
Rabies exposureZ20.3; add Z29.14 for HRIG, Z23 for the vaccine; a bite wound first
Rabies pre-exposure vaccinationZ23
Pertussis exposureZ20.818 (meningococcal: Z20.811)
Workplace asbestos exposureZ57.2, with Z77.090
Hepatitis B surveillanceZ11.59
Drug or alcohol test, post-offerZ02.1
Drug or alcohol test: suspicion, random, return-to-duty, follow-upZ02.89; Z02.83 for blood
Drug or alcohol test after an accidentThe injury first if treated, or Z04.2 if ruled out; then Z02.89 (Z02.83 for blood)
After a work accident, injury ruled outZ04.2

Z02.89 is only for an administrative exam with no code of its own; it isn't a catch-all.

Practice choice: DOT exam code

DOT exams are coded Z02.4, the Index's driving-license entry. Some providers use Z02.89. A payer's or contract's instruction overrides it.

Practice choice: TB screen code

A TB screen with no exposure is coded Z11.7, not Z11.1. A payer reading the tuberculin Index entry may expect Z11.1.

Practice choice: periodic exam code

A periodic exam of a current employee is coded Z02.89. Z02.1 is pre-employment only.

Practice choice: drug and alcohol test codes

The reason for the test sets the code. A post-offer test is Z02.1. Other administrative tests are Z02.89 for urine or breath, since Z02.83 names blood and no code names a urine or breath test. A positive result isn't coded at collection; the MRO reports it.
